This thesis employs a lighter formalism than the Metric First-Order Temporal Logic and Satisfiability Modulo Theories apparatus of Feng et al. (2023): a feasibility formulation over discretised time with one binary accessibility variable per audit record, in the constraint-modelling style of operations research. The justification is threefold. The conflict turns on a single semantic question, what “verifiable” means for an audit record, and a formulation that isolates that question communicates it more clearly than a general temporal-logic encoding. The lighter formulation is defensible at Master’s level by an author trained in logistics modelling rather than formal methods, which matters for the integrity of a thesis that must be owned and defended by its author. And the formulation is executable in ordinary Python, which makes the propositions checkable by a reader with no proof-assistant background. The cost of this choice is expressive power: the model cannot represent obligations whose structure exceeds the chosen formalism, a limitation recorded in [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) and revisited in Chapter 6.
## **3.4 Formal-Modelling Methodology**
This section states how the TRF Model is constructed. The model itself, with its full notation, propositions, and proofs, is developed in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg); what follows is the method by which it is built and the standard to which it is held.
*Step 1: Decomposition of the object.* Each cross-border audit record is decomposed into components that the regulatory instruments treat differently. The event metadata comprises the accountability content: which actor accessed which category of record, at what time, from which national contact point, under which legal basis and consent policy, with what outcome. Within the metadata, the accessor’s fields are separated from the link to the patient, because the two are reached by different obligations ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.3](#bookmark=id.b04xy7a2dxno)). The personal-data payload comprises the content of the exchanged clinical document. A cryptographic commitment binds the second to the first, so that the record can attest to what was accessed without retaining it in accessible form, and a key governs access to the payload. This decomposition is the modelling move on which everything else rests, and it is derived from the legal analysis of [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.3](#bookmark=id.8miqhq2ijj5t) rather than assumed: it is the necessity boundary of Article 17(3)(b), read with the minimisation principle of Article 5(1)(c), that separates what must be retained from what may not be.
*Step 2: Translation of each regime into a constraint.* Each regime is expressed as a constraint over discretised monthly time on the state of a record. The retention floor requires that the record remain verifiable throughout its retention window. The Article 17 erasure right requires that, following a valid erasure request, the personal-data payload cease to be accessible within the response period. The Article 68(12) deletion ceiling requires that, following permit expiry, payload accessibility cease within six months for records arising in the secondary-use pathway. The model is tri-lateral in the number of constraint types, not in the number of legal instruments it accommodates. The floor is a single parameterised constraint with two instances in the present setting: the ten-year minimum reported for cross-border audit repositories under the eHDSI deployment baseline, used as an illustrative value ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.3](#bookmark=id.b04xy7a2dxno)), and the one-year minimum imposed on Secure Processing Environment access logs by Article 73(1)(e) EHDS. Because the horizon is parameterised rather than hard-coded, the second instance required no structural change to the model, and jurisdiction-specific floors can be substituted on the same basis. The translation is documented claim by claim against the primary instruments, so that a reader can check each constraint against its source.
*Step 3: Definition of the competing semantics.* The pivotal move is to make explicit an assumption that the operational status quo leaves implicit. Under *plaintext-verifiability semantics*, a record satisfies the retention constraint only while its payload remains accessible in recoverable form. Under *accountability-preservation semantics*, a record satisfies the retention constraint while its metadata is intact, its commitment survives, and any invalidation event is itself recorded and witnessed. Both are candidate readings of what an audit repository is for; the thesis argues that the second is the reading the instruments actually require and the first is what an audit log that keeps its payload readable assumes.
*Step 4: Establishing the two results.* Proposition 1 states that under plaintext-verifiability semantics the constraint system is infeasible whenever an erasure request or a permit expiry falls within a record’s retention window, which, over a ten-year window, covers a request arriving in almost any month; how often requests in fact arrive is not modelled ([Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2)). The second floor instance makes the result sharper rather than weaker: where a one-year log-retention floor operates against a six-month deletion ceiling on the same environment, infeasibility under plaintext semantics arises from the two retention provisions alone, with no erasure request required to trigger it. Proposition 2 states that under accountability-preservation semantics the system is jointly satisfiable for every arrival pattern of erasure requests and permit expiries, and exhibits the mechanism that achieves this as the constructive witness. Two further results are obtained by the same method from the constraints rather than from the semantics: Proposition 3 states the exact condition under which a ceiling and a floor collide, and Proposition 4 states what relocating a record does to the ceiling and to the right. All four are argued informally at the level of rigour standard for design-science work rather than machine-checked; [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) records what that means for the strength of the claim.
*Step 5: Executable checking.* Because the formulation is light, both results can be checked by direct execution rather than only by argument. The checker described in [Section 3.6](#bookmark=id.o06sks8680nr) walks synthetic records through randomised arrivals of erasure requests and permit expiries and evaluates the constraints under each semantics in turn, producing violations under the first and none under the second. This does not constitute formal verification in the proof-assistant sense, and is not presented as such; it is a demonstration that the propositions hold on the instances examined, and its value is that it makes the argument inspectable by a reader who does not wish to take the proofs on trust.
## **3.5 Synthetic Data**
The demonstration requires patient records with realistic structure. No real patient data are used at any point in this thesis, and none were requested or obtained.
Synthetic records are generated using Synthea, an open-source synthetic patient generator that simulates the lifetime medical histories of statistically realistic but entirely fictional individuals, producing records in standard health-data formats (Walonoski et al., 2018).¹ Synthea is appropriate here for three reasons. Its output conforms to HL7 FHIR, the interoperability standard underlying the European Electronic Health Record Exchange Format. Its generation is seeded, so that a given seed reproduces a given population exactly. And it is established in the health-informatics literature as a substitute for real data in system-development contexts, which means its use requires no novel methodological defence.
Three configuration decisions are fixed, and one limitation of the generator must be recorded alongside them. The output conforms to *FHIR R4*, not R5, because the Norwegian national profile set (basisprofiler) maintained by HL7 Norway constrains R4; matching the Norwegian profile version is what makes the demonstration representative of the Norwegian setting rather than of a generic one. The population is approximately *one hundred synthetic patients*. That size is large enough to exercise the audit-record lifecycle across varied clinical encounter patterns and small enough to remain inspectable by hand when a result needs to be traced to its cause. Because the thesis reports no statistical inference, no power calculation governs this choice. And *random seeds are fixed and reported*, population seed and clinician seed both set to 20260915, so that the entire demonstration is reproducible from the thesis text.
The limitation concerns profiles rather than versions. Synthea’s default export conforms to the US Core implementation guide and draws its demographic, geographic, and care-pattern parameters from a United States population. The FHIR version therefore matches the version Norwegian basisprofiler constrain, but the profiles and the clinical content do not represent Norwegian practice, and this thesis makes no claim that they do. The consequence is bounded and is verified rather than assumed in [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.8](#bookmark=id.nkz790ri7jg7): because no constraint in the model reads the content of a payload, the demonstration’s results are invariant to payload provenance, and Norwegian representativeness is required of the *infrastructure analysis* in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) rather than of the generated records.
Synthea’s fidelity has been independently validated, and the validation bounds what may be claimed for it. Chen, Chun, Patel, Chiang, and James (2019) computed four clinical quality measures over a 1.2-million-patient Synthea cohort and compared them against publicly reported state and national rates. They found Synthea reliable in modelling demographics and the probability of services being offered, but limited in modelling heterogeneous health outcomes following intervention and in reproducing regional variation in care quality. These limitations do not, however, bear on the use made of Synthea in this thesis: the demonstration requires structurally valid FHIR resources and plausible encounter events from which audit records are generated, not accurate post-intervention outcome distributions. Had this thesis made epidemiological or clinical-effectiveness claims, the validation findings would be disqualifying; because it makes claims only about the behaviour of audit records under constraint, they are not.
The records themselves are not the object of study. They are the realism layer: the demonstration’s claims concern the behaviour of audit records and their cryptographic bindings under the three constraints, and the synthetic clinical data supply plausible content for the exchanges that generate those audit records. This distinction is important for interpreting the results reported in [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), and is restated there.
## **3.6 Sandbox Implementation Approach**
The sandbox is implemented in Python and has two layers, separated so that the load-bearing claim rests on the smaller and more inspectable component, and one optional module that reports no thesis figure.
The *feasibility checker* is the primary layer and the executable witness of the propositions. It constructs audit records as the tuples defined in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.3](#bookmark=id.b04xy7a2dxno), in two classes: cross-border audit records carrying the ten-year floor, and Secure Processing Environment access-log records carrying the one-year floor and the six-month ceiling. It then generates randomised arrivals of erasure requests and permit expiries across a monthly time horizon, and evaluates the three constraints under each semantics in turn, reporting violations. The two classes differ only in their floor parameter and in whether the ceiling applies, which is what makes them instances of one model rather than two models. The checker is kept small enough to be read and checked in full; [Table 5.1](#bookmark=id.bgo9ud2qcdks) gives its size. A reader who doubts Proposition 1 can find in its output the specific record, month, and constraint at which plaintext semantics fails; a reader who doubts Proposition 2 can confirm that no violation arises under invalidation semantics across the generated instances.
The *realism layer* wraps the checker so that its inputs derive from Synthea-generated FHIR bundles rather than from abstract record identifiers, computing commitments over the actual payloads and constructing metadata from the actual encounter events. It is smaller than the checker ([Table 5.1](#bookmark=id.bgo9ud2qcdks)) and is not load-bearing: if the wrapper were removed, the propositions and their executable check would stand unchanged. Its function is to demonstrate that the model’s abstractions correspond to the structure of real health-data artefacts rather than only to a convenient idealisation, and to test, by execution rather than assertion, whether any reported result depends on payload provenance.
Both layers, together with a demonstration viewer that executes them unmodified, are published in a public repository listed in Appendix A, so that the sandbox described here can be inspected and run rather than only read about.
Cryptographic operations use standard library primitives: salted commitments constructed with a standard hash function, and simulated key destruction implemented as irreversible removal of key material from the sandbox’s state. The commitments are hiding by construction, which isThe commitments are hiding by construction when salts are drawn at random (the reported run derives salts from the record identifier for reproducibility; see Appendix A, A.6), which is a design requirement rather than an implementation detail, since [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya) established that an unsalted hash of personal data may itself remain personal data. Every access event, invalidation and subject-link removal is appended to an append-only Merkle log, so that the verifiability condition can be checked as an inclusion proof that fails if an entry is altered. *No zero-knowledge proof system is implemented at any point*, and none is required. The mechanism’s verifiability rests on commitments, on the recorded invalidation event and on the log, not on succinct arguments. The optional module repeats the record lifecycle with real AES-256-GCM envelope encryption, to show that unreadability follows from key destruction rather than being asserted.
The constraint system is cross-checked on small instances by a separately written exhaustive search over every assignment of the accessibility variable, as an independent confirmation that the hand-written checker implements the constraints as stated ([Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.5](#bookmark=id.r6y2y1pct7yv)). This is a robustness measure rather than a component of the contribution.
What the sandbox does not do bounds what [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) may claim. It does not connect to any National Contact Point, real or test. It does not implement the OpenNCP transmission flow. It does not implement authentication or consent evaluation. It does not measure execution time, memory, throughput, or energy, and no such measurements are reported anywhere in this thesis.
## **3.7 Validity, Reliability, and Limitations**
The evaluation strategy is analytical rather than empirical, and its criteria are stated here in advance of the results.
*Internal validity* concerns whether the artefact is internally coherent: whether the constraints faithfully represent the instruments they translate, whether the two semantics are stated precisely enough to be distinguished, whether the propositions follow from the definitions, and whether the mechanism specified in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) is in fact the witness the feasibility result requires. This is assessed by argument and by the executable check of [Section 3.6](#bookmark=id.o06sks8680nr), and it is the axis on which the contribution principally stands or falls.
*External validity* concerns whether the artefact would fit the environment from which the problem was drawn. It is assessed by compatibility analysis against verified infrastructure: the audit-logging boundary of the MyHealth@EU transmission flow, the Norwegian NCPeH as it is now operating in live pilot, the Helsedataservice access pathway, the Norwegian Secure Processing Environment criteria in their hearing version, and the Secure Processing Environment specification published by TEHDAS2 during 2026 as deliverable D7.4. The last of these is a moving baseline: the binding requirements are to be laid down by Commission implementing acts due on 26 March 2027, after this thesis is submitted, so compatibility is assessed against the best-specified state of the infrastructure available at the time of writing rather than against its final form. The analysis is recorded requirement by requirement in [Table 4.1](#bookmark=id.ou2q52lu5vuw), each row naming its source, what the mechanism does, and whether the artefact executes it or meets it by specification. Compatibility analysis is weaker evidence than deployment, and is not presented as equivalent to it.
*Reliability* is addressed through determinism. Fixed seeds, reported parameters, and a fully specified checker mean that another researcher can reproduce every reported result exactly. Because no timing or performance claims are made, no repeated-run averaging is required.
Eight limitations are recorded at the outset rather than deferred to the conclusion, because each bounds what the later chapters may assert. This section is the canonical statement of them; later chapters refer back to it rather than restating it, and where a chapter adds a limitation specific to its own material it says so.
The first is the *proof standard*. The propositions are argued informally and checked executably on generated instances; they are not machine-checked, and the executable check confirms the results on the instances examined rather than establishing them for all instances. The claim made in this thesis is correspondingly bounded.
The second is the *expressiveness of the formalism*. The deliberate lightness described in [Section 3.3](#bookmark=id.mkgfiumlug0g) means the model cannot represent obligations whose structure exceeds a monthly-discretised binary-accessibility formulation: conditional obligations with complex temporal nesting, for instance, or interactions with instruments not included in the three modelled.
The third is the *key-destruction assumption*. The mechanism’s guarantees are conditional on honest and irreversible destruction of key material. As [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya) established through the secure-deletion literature, no approach operating above the storage medium can prove to an external observer that destruction occurred; the guarantee is conditional on a documented key-management boundary, which is the same condition the regulatory guidance on cryptographic unrecoverability imposes. This limitation is structural rather than incidental, and [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) engages the practitioner critique that builds on it.
The fourth is *scope*. The thesis models Union-level instruments and the Norwegian implementation; it does not model the national retention laws of other receiving jurisdictions, though the parameterisation of the retention horizon is designed to accommodate them. It addresses neither non-EEA jurisdictions nor the authentication and consent-propagation problems adjacent to the one examined.
The fifth is the *operational cost* of the mechanism. Per-record key granularity imposes a key-management burden that the thesis argues is bounded and auditable but does not quantify; [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.4](#bookmark=id.6dcjhrktbx5i) engages the critique and [Section 6.5](#bookmark=id.kbkvgbpgcwg5) sets out how the components scale.
The sixth concerns *interpretive authority*. Two steps in the argument rest on reasoning rather than on any regulatory holding: that an invalidated record continues to satisfy a retention obligation, and that Article 68(12) reaches the access logs a Secure Processing Environment generates where they are kept at patient-record granularity. [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.2](#bookmark=id.51bwj2518vrs) confronts both and [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8), [Section 7.4](#bookmark=id.ds5sargxa3ne) proposes how they would be settled.
The seventh and eighth are abstractions in the model itself, and they are stated because the model’s simplicity is what makes it defensible and also what bounds it.
The seventh is that the model treats every erasure request as valid. Article 17 is qualified: a controller may lawfully refuse a request where one of the exemptions in Article 17(3) applies, and in the audit setting many requests will be refused on exactly the Article 17(3)(b) ground the thesis discusses. A refused request imposes no erasure deadline, so the model, which treats every arriving request as triggering constraint C2, overstates how often erasure-driven collisions occur. It does not overstate whether they occur: Proposition 1 requires only that some valid request fall inside a retention window, and Corollary 1.2 involves no erasure request at all. The abstraction therefore inflates the frequencies reported in [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) and leaves the propositions untouched, which is why no result in this thesis is stated as a frequency.
The eighth is that the model represents a record’s payload as a single unit that is either readable or not. Real systems often erase at field level, redacting some elements of a record while retaining others, and a single binary accessibility variable cannot represent that. The simplification is conservative with respect to the propositions, since a mechanism that satisfies the constraints for a whole payload satisfies them for any subset of it, but it means the model says nothing about partial erasure, and a mechanism designed for field-level redaction would need a richer state space than the one used here.
## **3.8 Evaluation Design for the Next Cycle**
The evaluation reported in this thesis is analytical, as [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) sets out. Design Science Research also admits expert assessment as an evaluation method, and a specification-and-demonstration study of this kind commonly designs the evaluation that a subsequent cycle executes (Hevner, March, Park, & Ram, 2004; Peffers, Tuunanen, Rothenberger, & Chatterjee, 2007). That design has been produced and is specified in full in Appendix C.
The instrument comprises an eight-person expert panel drawn from four perspectives, two participants each: data protection, health IT architecture, Secure Processing Environment operation, and information logistics. Sessions last forty-five minutes, and participants describe current practice before being shown the proposed mechanism. A demonstration script runs the artefact live and states its limitations before participants are asked to find them. The instrument also includes a thirteen-question semi-structured interview guide, and a closed-response questionnaire of sixteen five-point Likert items across four dimensions: perceived utility, regulatory alignment, operational viability, and audit integrity. A thematic analysis plan sets out an explicit route by which findings would revise the trust model, the residue analysis, and the direction of the next design iteration.
Two features of the design matter here. Interview question seven asks practitioners directly whether Article 68(12) reaches the access logs an environment generates (the interpretive question on which Corollary 1.2 depends, identified in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb)) because practitioner readings of that provision are evidence this author cannot generate analytically. And the questionnaire pairs an item on what the mechanism lets an auditor verify, that an invalidation was logged and is unaltered, with an item on whether that attestation suffices without proof that the key was destroyed.
The instrument has not been executed. Executing it would process personal data about identifiable professionals, requiring notification to Sikt and a lead time of four to six weeks. It would also require revision of the scope statement in [Chapter 1](#bookmark=id.5f6pbrz60148), [Section 1.5](#bookmark=id.cdgu1valy2l8), of [Section 3.9](#bookmark=id.ejbxnttnoczq) below, and of the Declaration of Originality, each of which states that this research involves no human participants. Those statements are accurate for the thesis as submitted. [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8), [Section 7.5](#bookmark=id.clphjrvscppc) carries execution of this instrument as the immediate next step in the research programme.
## **3.9 Ethical Considerations**
The ethical profile of this thesis is unusually simple, and the simplicity is a consequence of deliberate design choices rather than an absence of reflection.
No personal data are processed at any stage. All records are synthetically generated and describe no real individual. No human participants are involved: no interviews, surveys, observations, or usability studies were conducted, and no data about identifiable persons were collected. Consequently no approval from the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research, from a regional research-ethics committee, or from any institutional review board was required, and none is claimed.
The choice of synthetic data is itself ethically grounded rather than merely convenient, and the grounding rests on a Norwegian supervisory decision rather than on commentary. The relevant decision is that of 11 May 2021, in which the Norwegian Data Protection Authority imposed an administrative fine of NOK 1,250,000 on the Norwegian Confederation of Sports (Norges idrettsforbund). The authority held that the organisation had no lawful basis for testing a cloud migration using the personal data of 3.2 million individuals. It reasoned that processing must be necessary for its purpose, and that the purpose could not be pursued where it was achievable by less privacy-invasive means; it further found the scale of personal data used in testing to be unnecessary (Datatilsynet, 2021). The general position that testing should proceed on anonymised or, preferably, synthetic data, attributed to both the Norwegian authority and the European Data Protection Supervisor, is set out in the Norwegian professional literature summarising this line of practice (Deloitte Advokatfirma, 2020). A thesis that proposes a mechanism for protecting personal data in audit trails would sit poorly with itself if it used real patient data to demonstrate that mechanism. The methodological choice and the ethical position coincide.
Two further commitments govern the reporting of results. Every claim of fact is traceable to a retrievable primary source, and where verification remains incomplete the incompleteness is flagged rather than smoothed over. No quantitative result is reported that was not produced by the procedures described in this chapter, and no capability is claimed that was not built: the components excluded from scope in [Chapter 1](#bookmark=id.5f6pbrz60148), [Section 1.5](#bookmark=id.cdgu1valy2l8) are described as future work and never as achievements.
¹ Synthea is documented in Walonoski et al. (2018), *Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association*, 25(3), 230–238, https://doi.org/10.1093/jamia/ocx079.
# **Chapter 4. The Tri-Lateral Retention Feasibility Model and the Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation Mechanism**
*Proposition statements and proofs in this chapter are the author’s own. Regulatory claims are anchored to the primary instruments cited at each point.*
## **4.1 Purpose and Structure of the Chapter**
This chapter contains the analytical core of the thesis. It does three things in sequence, and the sequence matters because each step licenses the next.
First, it establishes what the law actually requires to be retained, as distinct from what an audit log may happen to retain. This is the necessity analysis begun in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.3](#bookmark=id.8miqhq2ijj5t), and it produces the decomposition on which the model rests.
Second, it constructs the Tri-Lateral Retention Feasibility (TRF) Model: a formal representation of the retention regimes as constraints over discretised time, together with two candidate semantics for what it means for an audit record to be verifiable. Within that model it states and proves four results. Proposition 1 establishes that under plaintext-verifiability semantics the constraint system is infeasible. Proposition 2 establishes that under an alternative semantics the system is jointly satisfiable, and its proof is constructive: it exhibits the mechanism that achieves satisfaction. Proposition 3 states exactly when a deletion ceiling collides with a retention floor and what the ceiling’s anchor decides, and Proposition 4 shows why moving a record out of the regulated environment, the most direct rival design, meets the ceiling but not the right to erasure.
Third, it specifies that mechanism, Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation, in enough detail to be implemented, analyses the residue it leaves behind against the legal threshold that residue must clear, compares it against rival designs, and maps it onto the Norwegian infrastructure verified in Chapter 2.
The order of exposition follows the order in which the thesis has developed the problem: the cross-border primary-use case is treated first throughout, with the Secure Processing Environment case following as the second and sharper instance.
A note on what the propositions are and are not. They are mathematical statements about a model, proved informally at the standard of rigour normal for design-science work, and checked executably in Chapter 5. They are not machine-checked, and they are not claims about the world independent of the model’s fidelity. Their force depends entirely on whether the constraints faithfully translate the instruments, which is why [Section 4.2](#bookmark=id.czwt0vfyycw5) documents that translation claim by claim rather than asserting it.
## **4.2 What Must Be Retained: The Necessity Analysis**
The decomposition that makes the model possible is not a modelling convenience. It is derived from the legal position established in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.3](#bookmark=id.8miqhq2ijj5t), and everything downstream inherits it.
Article 17(3)(b) GDPR exempts from erasure processing that is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation. The audit-retention obligations are such obligations. But the exemption is bounded by necessity, and Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing. The question is therefore not whether an audit record may be retained, but which parts of it necessity protects.
The purpose that the retention obligations serve is accountability: establishing, after the fact, that a particular access occurred, by whom, when, under what authority, and with what result. That purpose is served by the event metadata. It is not served by continued controller access to personal data the record carries beyond those attributes: the demographic content of the logged query, or, where a deployment keeps it, the content of the document that was exchanged. A supervisory authority investigating whether a Spanish clinician’s access to a Norwegian patient summary in March 2027 was lawful needs to know that the access occurred, which clinician performed it, under which eIDAS assertion, against which consent policy, and whether it succeeded. It does not need the patient’s name and birth date as typed into the query, still less the patient’s medication list, to answer that question.
This yields the central claim of the necessity analysis: *the accountability function of a cross-border audit record is discharged by its metadata and by a binding commitment to its payload, and does not require the payload to remain accessible.* Retention of accessible plaintext payload for ten years therefore exceeds what Article 17(3)(b) protects. Article 5(1)(c) positively requires that it not be retained where the purpose can be achieved without it.
Two sources support it and one limits it. The Norwegian Data Protection Authority’s internal-control guidance places exactly this weighing on the controller, requiring determination of lawful retention periods and deletion deadlines through explicit balancing of purpose, business need, and both retention rights and retention duties (Datatilsynet, n.d.-a). The Authority’s privacy-by-design guidance equates anonymisation with deletion (Datatilsynet, n.d.-b), which is what permits a transformed record to satisfy an erasure obligation at all. The limit is that the same Authority sets a high threshold for when data cease to be personal: encryption protects data rather than rendering them unidentifiable, and data remain personal while any key or linkage capable of re-identification is retained (Datatilsynet, 2015). The residue left by the mechanism must therefore be analysed against that threshold rather than assumed to clear it, which is the work of [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s).
## **4.3 The Model: Objects and Notation**
Let the time domain be discretised into months, indexed by $t\in N$, with $t=0$ the month in which the system begins operation. Monthly granularity is chosen because every obligation in the system is expressed in months or years, and because the shortest deadline in the system, the erasure response period, is one month.
Let $A$ be the set of audit records. Each record $a\in A$ is generated by a single access event and is represented as a tuple
$a=\left({ m\left({a}\right), p\left({a}\right), c\left({a}\right), k\left({a}\right), t\left({a}\right), F\left({a}\right), \sigma \left({a}\right) }\right)$
where:
  - $m\left({a}\right)$ma is the *event metadata*: the actor identifier, the actor’s national contact point, the patient pseudonym, the document category accessed, the legal basis and consent policy applied, the timestamp, and the outcome. Metadata contains no clinical content. It is partitioned as $m\left({a}\right)={m}_{acc}\left({a}\right)\cup {m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$. The *accessor fields* ${m}_{acc}\left({a}\right)$ record who acted, when, under which legal basis or permit, and with what outcome. The *subject fields* ${m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$ relate the event to a data subject: the patient pseudonym and any reference to that subject’s records. The partition does work only in the Secure Processing Environment case ([Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb)).
  - $p\left({a}\right)$ is the *personal-data payload*: <comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4ec>the personal data the record carries beyond what accountability requires<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4ec> ([Section 4.2](#bookmark=id.czwt0vfyycw5)). Its content depends on the record class. For a cross-border record it is the identifying content of the logged query. The IHE Cross Gateway Patient Discovery transaction (ITI-55), by which one country’s gateway locates a patient in another, requires the person’s name and birth time unless an identifier is supplied, and requires both gateways to record the query segment, base64-encoded, in the audit message’s ParticipantObjectQuery field (IHE International, 2024, Sections 3.55.4.1.2.1 and 3.55.5.1). The audit record therefore holds the patient’s demographic query and not only a pseudonym. This is the transaction on which the patient-identification step of the MyHealth@EU flow rests ([Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.2](#bookmark=id.mfssrs4fkidd)); the eHDSI audit specification that profiles it was not available to this thesis, so the IHE requirement is taken as the baseline any profile starts from. For a Secure Processing Environment record it is the content of the logged activity, where the environment logs at that level: the text and parameters of the query or command run against the permitted dataset, and any output retained with the entry. The Joint Action’s specification requires these logs to cover “access to electronic health data” and “data import, export, or release of outputs” and fixes no fields (TEHDAS2, 2026, Table 5.4, OPR-17, p. 51); whatever an environment records under those headings beyond the accessor fields is $p\left({a}\right)$. The model does not require $p\left({a}\right)$ to be a clinical document, only personal data that the accountability purpose does not need.
  - $c\left({a}\right)$ is a *commitment* to the payload, $c\left({a}\right)$ = Commit($p\left({a}\right),r\left({a}\right)$), where $r\left({a}\right)$ is a per-record random salt. The commitment scheme is required to be *hiding* (the commitment reveals nothing about the payload to an adversary without the salt) and *binding* (no second payload can be opened against the same commitment). The requirement that it be hiding rather than a bare hash is a consequence of [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s) and is not optional.
  - $k\left({a}\right)$ is the *payload key*: the key material under which $p\left({a}\right)$ is stored.
  - $t\left({a}\right)$ is the month in which the access event occurred.
  - $F\left({a}\right)\in N$ is the *retention floor* applying to the record, expressed in months.
  - $\sigma \left({a}\right)\in \{primary,secondary\}$ is the *pathway* in which the record arose.
The floor is a parameter of the record rather than a constant of the model. The form is taken from chain-of-custody practice in physical cross-border logistics, where a consignment carries one custody record whose retention parameter is set by whichever jurisdiction’s regime governs it, rather than a separate ledger per jurisdiction; [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.7](#bookmark=id.78e6qn6q5oox) sets out the correspondence. In the present setting it takes two values:
  - $F\left({a}\right)=120$Fa=120 for cross-border audit records held in ATNA-compliant audit repositories, <comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4ew>this being the ten-year minimum reported as the eHDSI deployment baseline<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4ew> for MyHealth@EU operations (Simjanoska Misheva et al., 2025). The value is illustrative: the primary agreement inspected requires audit trails without stating a period (eHealth Network, 2017, clause II.4.2), and by Corollary 2.2 no result depends on it. The IHE ATNA profile itself prescribes no retention period; the floor arises from the deployment binding, and the model is correct only if this distinction is preserved.
  - $F\left({a}\right)=12$ for access and activity logs of Secure Processing Environments, this being the one-year minimum imposed by Article 73(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2025/327 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025). The Joint Action’s specification recommends five years (TEHDAS2, 2026, Table 5.4, OPR-18, p. 51); by Proposition 3 a longer floor enlarges the set of records whose permit expiry falls inside it, and by Corollary 2.2 no result depends on the value.
Two event processes act on records. An *erasure request* arrives for record $a$ at month ${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)$ if the data subject exercises Article 17 in respect of the personal data underlying that record; if no request arrives, ${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)=\infty $. A *permit expiry* occurs at month ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)$ for records with $\sigma \left({a}\right)$ = secondary, being the month in which the data permit under which the processing occurred expires; for primary-pathway records ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)=\infty $.
Finally, let $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)\in \{0,1\}$ be the *payload-accessibility variable*: $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=1$ if the controller can recover $p\left({a}\right)$ in intelligible form at month $t$, and 0 otherwise. This single binary variable per record per month is the entire state space of the model, and its minimality is deliberate: the conflict turns on exactly one question, which is whether the payload is readable, and a formulation that admits no other state variable cannot obscure that question behind modelling detail. The cost of that minimality is that the model cannot represent field-level redaction, where some elements of a payload are erased and others retained; [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) records this as a stated abstraction.
The Secure Processing Environment case needs one further variable, and only on the reading of Article 68(12) that [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb) identifies. Let $\beta \left({a,t}\right)\in \{0,1\}$ be the *subject-link variable*: $\beta \left({a,t}\right)=1$ if the subject fields ${m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$ can be read in the environment at month $t$, and 0 otherwise. Where that reading does not apply, $\beta $ is unconstrained and plays no part in any result.
Let $V\left({a,t}\right)\in \{0,1\}$ denote whether record $a$ *counts as verifiable* at month $t$. $V$ is not defined yet; defining it is the subject of [Section 4.5](#bookmark=id.4cz2aajv8qbr), and the two competing definitions are what the propositions distinguish.
## **4.4 The Three Constraints**
Each regime is now expressed as a constraint on the trajectory of $\alpha $ and $V$.
*C1: Retention floor.* For every record $a$ and every month $t$ with $t\left({a}\right)\leq t\leq t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right)$:
$V\left({a,t}\right)=1  \forall  t\in \left[{ t\left({a}\right), t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right) }\right]$
The record must count as verifiable throughout its retention window. The window is closed at both ends and so spans $F+1$ monthly indices. This is deliberate: the obligations are minimums (“at least one year”), and a record written during month $t\left({a}\right)$ completes $F$ full months only during month $t\left({a}\right)+F$, so requiring verifiability through that month is the conservative reading of “at least”. A half-open window would shorten every obligation by up to a month. Source: the eHDSI deployment baseline as reported, an illustrative value, for $F=120$; Article 73(1)(e) EHDS for $F=12$.
*C2: Erasure right.* For every record $a$ for which a valid erasure request arrives at ${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)<\infty $, and for every month $t\geq {t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta $:
$\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0  \forall  t\geq {t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta $
The payload must cease to be accessible within the response period $\delta $. Source: Article 17(1) GDPR, with $\delta $ determined by Article 12(3) GDPR, which requires the controller to act without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests provided the data subject is informed within the first month. The model takes $\delta =1$ as the baseline and admits $\delta =3$ as the extended case; results are stated for arbitrary finite $\delta $ and do not depend on which is chosen. Constraint C2 is triggered only by a *valid* request. The model does not represent the Article 17(3) exemptions under which a controller may lawfully refuse, and so treats every arriving request as valid; [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) explains why this affects the frequencies reported in [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) but not the propositions.
*C3: Deletion ceiling.* For every record $a$ with $\sigma \left({a}\right)$ = secondary and every month $t\geq {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$:
$\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0  \forall  t\geq {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$
and, where the record’s subject fields are electronic health data within the environment ([Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb)),
$\beta \left({a,t}\right)=0  \forall  t\geq {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$
Electronic health data must not remain in the Secure Processing Environment more than six months after permit expiry. Source: Article 68(12) EHDS, which provides that “the electronic health data within the secure processing environment shall be deleted within six months of the expiry of the data permit” (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025), as operationalised by TEHDAS2 (2025).
The structural asymmetry between C1 on one hand and C2–C3 on the other is the whole problem. C1 is a lower bound on the persistence of a property; C2 and C3 are upper bounds on the persistence of accessibility. Whether they conflict depends entirely on whether $V$ is defined in terms of $\alpha $, which is the question [Section 4.5](#bookmark=id.4cz2aajv8qbr) makes explicit.
## **4.5 Two Semantics of Verifiability**
*Semantics I: plaintext verifiability.* A record counts as verifiable exactly when its payload is accessible:
${V}^{I}\left({a,t}\right)=\alpha \left({a,t}\right)$
This is the semantics of an audit log that keeps what was accessed readable for as long as it keeps the record. Under it, an audit record whose payload cannot be produced is treated as an incomplete or broken record, and audit integrity is understood as the continued producibility of what was accessed. <comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4es>How common such logs are is not established here.<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4es> What is established is that nothing in the instruments rules them out and that the cross-border profile supplies their content, since ITI-55 requires both gateways to record the patient’s demographic query ([Section 4.3](#bookmark=id.b04xy7a2dxno)). No instrument states this semantics, and none states the alternative.
*Semantics II: accountability-preserving verifiability.* A record counts as verifiable when its accountability content is intact and any loss of payload accessibility is itself accounted for:
${V}^{II}\left({a,t}\right)=1\Leftrightarrow (i)\wedge (ii)\wedge (iii)$
where, at month $t$: (i) ${m}_{acc}\left({a}\right)$ is intact and unmodified, and so is ${m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$ unless its removal is recorded under (iii); (ii) $c\left({a}\right)$ is present and binding; and (iii) if $\alpha \left({a,t′}\right)=1$ for some $t′<t$ and $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$, or likewise for $\beta $, then an invalidation entry $\iota \left({a}\right)$ recording the transition, its month, its legal ground, and its authorising actor, is present in the audit trail and is itself covered by (i).
Under Semantics II an audit record that has lost its payload is not a broken record. It is a complete record of an access event *and* of the lawful invalidation of that event’s payload. The audit trail grows rather than shrinks when erasure occurs.
Neither semantics is stipulated by the instruments. [Section 4.10](#bookmark=id.2c8thzi7kbd9) argues that Semantics II is the better reading of what the instruments require; the propositions below establish what follows from each.
## **4.6 Propositions 1 and 3: Infeasibility, and Where the Ceiling Is Anchored**
*Proposition 1.* Under Semantics I, the constraint system $\{C1,C2,C3\}$ is infeasible for any record $a$ such that
${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta \leq t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right) or {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6\leq t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right).$
*Proof.* Take a record $a$ satisfying the first disjunct, and let ${t}^{*}={t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta $. By hypothesis ${t}^{*}\leq t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right)$, and since erasure requests arrive after the access that generates the record, ${t}^{*}\geq t\left({a}\right)$. Hence ${t}^{*}$ lies within the retention window, so C1 requires $V\left({a,{t}^{*}}\right)=1$. Under Semantics I, ${V}^{I}\left({a,{t}^{*}}\right)=\alpha \left({a,{t}^{*}}\right)$, so C1 requires $\alpha \left({a,{t}^{*}}\right)=1$. But C2 requires $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$ for all $t\geq {t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta ={t}^{*}$, so C2 requires $\alpha \left({a,{t}^{*}}\right)=0$. The two requirements are contradictory, and no assignment of $\alpha $ satisfies both. The argument for the second disjunct is identical with ${t}^{*}={t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$ and C3 in place of C2. ∎
*Corollary 1.1 (cross-border case).* For cross-border audit records, $F\left({a}\right)=120$. The system is infeasible for record $a$ whenever an erasure request arrives at any month ${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)\leq t\left({a}\right)+120$ − $\delta $: that is, at any point in the first nine years and eleven months of a ten-year window under the baseline response period. The condition is therefore not one of unusual timing: it holds for a request arriving in any but the last month of the window. How often data subjects exercise Article 17 is an empirical question that the model does not answer ([Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2)).
*Corollary 1.2 (Secure Processing Environment case).* For Secure Processing Environment access logs, $F\left({a}\right)=12$ and $\sigma \left({a}\right)$ = secondary. Suppose the permit expires at or before the sixth month of the record’s retention window, so that ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6\leq t\left({a}\right)+12$. Then C1 and C3 are contradictory at ${t}^{*}={t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$ by the argument above, provided C3 reaches the record. *Where it does, no erasure request is required.* It does so when the log entry is itself electronic health data within the environment, which, on the reading set out below, is the case for logs kept at patient-record granularity and not for logs kept at dataset granularity. For such records the infeasibility follows from two provisions of a single regulation acting on a single environment. Article 73(1)(e) requires the identifiable log to remain verifiable for twelve months, and Article 68(12) requires the electronic health data within the environment to be deleted six months after permit expiry. Where the remaining permit duration at the time the log is written is six months or less, the two windows necessarily overlap. The model makes no claim about how often this occurs in practice; the collision’s existence, not its frequency, is what Corollary 1.2 asserts.
Where it holds, Corollary 1.2 is the sharpest form of the thesis’s problem statement.Corollary 1.2 is a conditional extension of the problem statement; the request-driven conflict of Corollary 1.1 does not depend on it. It shows that the conflict does not depend on the exercise of a data-subject right, on the eHDSI deployment baseline, or on any synthesis across instruments of differing legal weight. It is internal to Regulation (EU) 2025/327.
*The interpretive condition on which Corollary 1.2 depends.* The corollary holds if, and only if, the deletion obligation of Article 68(12) reaches the identifiable access logs that Article 73(1)(e) requires to be kept. That condition is contestable and is stated as such.
Article 68(12) provides that “the electronic health data within the secure processing environment shall be deleted within six months of the expiry of the data permit”. Its scope is set by location rather than by provenance: it does not say “the data made available under the data permit”. Its object, however, is electronic health data, which Article 2(2)(a) and (c) define as “data concerning health and genetic data, processed in an electronic form”, personal or non-personal. An access log is therefore not reached merely because it sits within the environment. An entry recording that an authorised researcher opened a dataset at a given time concerns the researcher, not anyone’s health, and Article 73(1) ties the identifiability of logs to the persons who access: access is restricted to “authorised natural persons listed in the data permit” (point (a)), and the handling of data to “authorised identifiable individuals” (point (c)). The Joint Action’s specification for these environments reads Article 73(1)(e) the same way: “All SPE logs MUST identify the actor” (TEHDAS2, 2026, Table 5.1, EHDSR-7, p. 31). An entry kept at patient-record granularity is different. Recording that a named patient’s record in a disease cohort was accessed reveals that the patient belongs to the cohort, which is data concerning health. Such entries are electronic health data within the environment, and on the broad reading, which takes the provision’s scope from its location, Article 68(12) reaches them, and Corollary 1.2 follows for them.
<comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4eo>The contextual case for the narrow reading<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4eo> is that the provision sits within the data-permit article, adjacent to provisions on permit duration, extension, and storage fees, and that the mischief it addresses is the indefinite retention of permitted datasets after the purpose that justified them has lapsed. The rest of the paragraph supports this: it concerns the cost of storing the dataset, “a storage system with reduced capabilities”, and “the formula for the creation of the requested dataset”. On that reading the obligation attaches to the permit dataset, the access logs fall outside it, and no collision between Articles 68(12) and 73(1)(e) arises.
This thesis states Corollary 1.2 conditionally, for logs kept at patient-record granularity on the broad reading, and gives the grounds for both readings rather than choosing one by assertion. Little turns on which reading prevails. Under the narrow reading, Corollary 1.2 lapses, and with it the claim that infeasibility arises without any data-subject action. Proposition 1 itself is untouched, because its first disjunct concerns erasure requests rather than permit expiry: identifiable access logs remain personal data whoever provided them, they remain within the scope of Article 17, and a request arriving inside the twelve-month floor collides with Article 73(1)(e) exactly as the cross-border case collides with the eHDSI floor. Corollary 1.1 is untouched entirely. Proposition 2, the mechanism, and the residue analysis are untouched, since they are indifferent to which instrument generates the deadline.
The narrow reading, or logs kept at dataset granularity, therefore cost the thesis its sharpest instance and none of its results. The broad reading, for logs kept at patient-record granularity, adds a collision that requires no data subject to act, and Proposition 2 resolves it without choosing between the readings, because the accessor fields that Article 73(1)(e) requires to be identifiable are not the subject fields that Article 68(12) may reach ([Section 4.7](#bookmark=id.qemvcyvw7sy2)). [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) treats the resolution of this interpretive question as a matter for supervisory authority rather than for this author, alongside the authority question concerning verifiability itself.
*Where the ceiling is anchored.* Corollary 1.2 and the cross-sector instance of [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.10](#bookmark=id.odezbdc5356l) are both cases of one condition, the structural content of the problem rather than a property of either instrument.
*Proposition 3 (anchoring).* Let a record’s floor of $F$ months run from its creation month $t\left({a}\right)$, and let a ceiling of $L$ months run from an event at month $e\left({a}\right)\geq t\left({a}\right)$. Under Semantics I, the floor and the ceiling are jointly satisfiable for $a$ if and only if $e\left({a}\right)+L>t\left({a}\right)+F$. Hence (i) if the ceiling is anchored to the same event as the floor, $e\left({a}\right)=t\left({a}\right)$, they are satisfiable for every record if and only if $L>F$, a condition decidable from the text alone; and (ii) if the ceiling is anchored to an external event, then whenever $L\leq F$ they fail for exactly those records with $e\left({a}\right)-t\left({a}\right)\leq F-L$, a set that the text does not reveal and each record’s history determines.
*Proof.* C1 under Semantics I requires $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=1$ for every month $t$ up to $t\left({a}\right)+F$; the ceiling requires $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$ for every $t\geq e\left({a}\right)+L$. Since $e\left({a}\right)+L\geq t\left({a}\right)$, some month of the window carries both demands if and only if $e\left({a}\right)+L\leq t\left({a}\right)+F$. Cases (i) and (ii) substitute $e\left({a}\right)=t\left({a}\right)$ and rearrange. ∎
The proposition corrects as well as formalises. A collision needs a ceiling no longer than the floor whichever way it is anchored; what the anchor decides is whether the collision can be seen. A provision that measured both limits from one event and set the ceiling inside the floor would contradict itself on its face. Section 17 of politiregisterloven, a floor of twelve months and a ceiling of thirty-six from the same log entry, does not ([Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.10](#bookmark=id.odezbdc5356l)). A ceiling measured from an external event can sit inside the floor with no visible contradiction, because whether the two clocks cross depends on when that event falls for each record. Article 68(12) is of the second kind: six months from permit expiry against twelve months from the log entry, with the collision arising for exactly the records whose permit expires within six months of the entry, which is the condition of Corollary 1.2. The diagnostic question for any candidate instance is therefore whether a ceiling no longer than the floor is anchored to an event other than the one the floor runs from.
## **4.7 Proposition 2: Feasibility under Accountability-Preserving Verifiability**
*Proposition 2.* Under Semantics II, the constraint system $\{C1,C2,C3\}$ is jointly satisfiable for every record $a\in A$, for every arrival pattern of erasure requests $\{{t}_{r}\left({a}\right)\}$ and permit expiries $\{{t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)\}$, and for every floor parameter $F\left({a}\right)\in N$.
*Proof (constructive).* Define the following trajectory for an arbitrary record $a$. Let
${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)=min\left({ {t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta ,  {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6 }\right)$
be the *invalidation month*, with the convention min($\infty ,\infty )=\infty $. Construct the trajectory:
1.  For $t<{t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$: set $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=1$. Retain $m\left({a}\right),c\left({a}\right),k\left({a}\right)$, and $p\left({a}\right)$.
2.  At $t={t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$, if finite: destroy $k\left({a}\right)$ irreversibly; <comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4eg>where the ground is Article 68(12) and C3 reaches the subject fields, remove<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4eg> ${m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$ as well and set $\beta \left({a,t}\right)=0$; append to the audit trail an invalidation entry $\iota \left({a}\right)$ recording the month, the legal ground (Article 17(1) or Article 68(12) as applicable), what was removed, and the authorising actor; retain ${m}_{acc}\left({a}\right)$ and $c\left({a}\right)$ unchanged.
3.  For $t>{t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$: set $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$, and $\beta \left({a,t}\right)=0$ where step 2 removed the subject fields. Retain ${m}_{acc}\left({a}\right),c\left({a}\right)$, and $\iota \left({a}\right)$.
4.  If C3 reaches the subject fields and ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)<{t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$, so that an erasure request fixed the invalidation month, remove ${m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$ at ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$, set $\beta \left({a,t}\right)=0$ from that month, and append a second entry to $\iota \left({a}\right)$ recording it.
It must be shown that this trajectory satisfies all three constraints.
*C2 is satisfied.* If ${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)<\infty $ then ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)\leq {t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta $ by construction, and by steps 2–3, $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$ for all $t\geq {t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$, hence for all $t\geq {t}_{r}\left({a}\right)+\delta $. If ${t}_{r}\left({a}\right)=\infty $, C2 is vacuous.
*C3 is satisfied.* If $\sigma \left({a}\right)$ = secondary and ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)<\infty $ then ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)\leq {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$, and by the same steps $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$ for all $t\geq {t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$, and $\beta \left({a,t}\right)=0$ from the same month wherever C3 reaches the subject fields. If ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$ was set by an earlier erasure request, step 4 removes the subject fields at ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$. Otherwise C3 is vacuous.
*C1 is satisfied.* Let $t$ be any month in the retention window, $t\left({a}\right)\leq t\leq t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right)$. Condition (i) holds because no step of the construction modifies or removes ${m}_{acc}\left({a}\right)$, and the only removal of ${m}_{subj}\left({a}\right)$ is recorded in $\iota \left({a}\right)$. Condition (ii) holds because no step removes $c\left({a}\right)$; the commitment is not derived from $k\left({a}\right)$ and its persistence is unaffected by key destruction. For condition (iii): if $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=1$ the condition is vacuous; if $\alpha \left({a,t}\right)=0$ then $t\geq {t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$, and step 2 has placed $\iota \left({a}\right)$ in the audit trail, where step 3 retains it, and $\iota \left({a}\right)$ is covered by (i). Hence ${V}^{II}\left({a,t}\right)=1$ throughout the window. The terminal transition of [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv) takes place after the window and is not part of this trajectory.
All three constraints are satisfied, for arbitrary arrival times and arbitrary $F\left({a}\right)$. ∎
*Corollary 2.1.* The construction requires no coordination between the erasure process and the retention process, and no knowledge at the time a record is created of whether an erasure request will ever arrive. The invalidation month is determined entirely by events as they occur.
*Corollary 2.2.* Because $F\left({a}\right)$ is arbitrary in the proof, the result holds simultaneously for the ten-year cross-border floor and the one-year Secure Processing Environment floor, and for any national floor substituted for either. The model is tri-lateral in constraint type and indifferent to the number of floor instances.
*A note on what kind of result this is.* The results of this chapter are stated as propositions rather than theorems, because their proofs are short once the semantics are fixed. The weight of the argument lies elsewhere: in [Section 4.2](#bookmark=id.czwt0vfyycw5)’s necessity analysis, which justifies Semantics II, and in Propositions 3 and 4, which say where the conflict arises and where cryptography is necessary. One objection is that Proposition 2 proves little, because Semantics II was defined in full knowledge of the trajectory that satisfies it. The objection has force and the response is to concede its premise and deny its conclusion. The mathematical content of Proposition 2 is indeed modest: once verifiability is decoupled from payload accessibility, the existence of a satisfying trajectory is close to immediate, and the proof is a verification rather than a discovery. But the substantive claim of this chapter was never that a satisfying trajectory exists under some semantics; any number of semantics would admit one, including trivial semantics under which every record counts as verifiable always. The claim is that *this* semantics is a defensible reading of what the retention obligations require, grounded in the necessity boundary of Article 17(3)(b), the minimisation principle of Article 5(1)(c), and the accountability purpose the obligations serve. It is also the weakest departure from plaintext verifiability that achieves feasibility, preserving every element of the audit record that the accountability purpose needs and discarding only what it does not. Proposition 1 carries the load that Proposition 2 does not: it establishes that *some* departure is unavoidable, because the status quo admits no solution at all. Proposition 2 then shows that a principled and minimal departure suffices. The legal defensibility of Semantics II is argued in [Section 4.2](#bookmark=id.czwt0vfyycw5) and its want of authority is confronted in [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.2](#bookmark=id.51bwj2518vrs); it is not established by the proposition, and no reader should take the proposition as establishing it.
*What the proposition does and does not establish.* It establishes that the constraint system as formalised admits a solution, and exhibits one. It does not establish that the exhibited solution is lawful (that depends on whether the residue it leaves clears the legal threshold, which [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s) addresses) nor that key destruction can be verified by an external party, which [Section 4.10](#bookmark=id.2c8thzi7kbd9) concedes it cannot. The invalidation entry specified in [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv) is an *attested* record of destruction, not a *proof* of it; the proof-of-secure-erasure and certified-deletion literatures reviewed in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.4](#bookmark=id.3sdtdkmqwjlq) mark that boundary, and [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) treats it as the outer limit of the contribution. Proposition 2 is a mathematical result about a model, and its value is that it converts a question that has been debated qualitatively into one with a definite answer under stated assumptions.
## **4.8 The Mechanism: Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation**
The trajectory constructed in the proof of Proposition 2 is the specification of the mechanism. This section states it as an implementable design.
*Key hierarchy.* Each record’s payload is encrypted under a per-record data key $k\left({a}\right)$. Per-record rather than per-subject or per-dataset granularity is required because the invalidation events of Proposition 2 occur at record granularity: a permit expiry invalidates the records of one permit, while an erasure request invalidates the records relating to one data subject, and these sets intersect without nesting. Data keys are themselves held under a key-encrypting key in a hardware security module or equivalent custody boundary. Destruction of $k\left({a}\right)$ is effected by destruction of the wrapped data key and any cached copies, within the documented custody boundary. This is the hierarchy that key-management guidance prescribes, in which data keys are protected by key-encrypting keys and destruction means removing “all traces of a cryptographic key so that it cannot be recovered by either physical or electronic means” (Barker, 2020, [Section 2.1](#bookmark=id.qlxjdv9l0chh)). The optional module of the artefact executes it: per-record 256-bit data keys under AES in Galois/Counter Mode (Dworkin, 2007), each wrapped under a key-encrypting key and destroyed at the record’s invalidation month (Appendix A, A.15). The custody object stands in for a hardware security module, so destruction there is destruction in program memory.
*Ciphertext.* At ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$ the ciphertext of $p\left({a}\right)$ is deleted from the audit store together with $k\left({a}\right)$. Nothing in Semantics II uses it once the key is gone, and deleting it removes the exposure that a retained ciphertext would carry to future cryptanalytic capability, quantum capability included, over the rest of a ten-year floor ([Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s)). Key destruction remains the operative erasure for copies the store cannot delete at once, such as replicas and backups: they become unreadable at ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$ and leave by ordinary rotation. The specification for Secure Processing Environments accepts exactly this: electronic health data “MUST be deleted or rendered unrecoverable within six months of permit expiry, including any backups or redundant copies” (TEHDAS2, 2026, Table 5.2, OPR-6, p. 43). The same requirement continues: deletion must proceed “while ensuring compliance with applicable legal obligations and traceability or reproducibility requirements where relevant”, and its rationale leaves it to “the deletion and retention policy” to “balance these obligations”. The specification asks for the balance and does not say how it is struck; for the logs, this mechanism is one way to strike it.
*Commitment.* $c\left({a}\right)$ = Commit($p\left({a}\right),r\left({a}\right)$) with a per-record salt $r\left({a}\right)$. The salt is stored with the metadata until invalidation and is destroyed together with $k\left({a}\right)$ at ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$. Before invalidation it lets an auditor open the commitment against the payload. After invalidation no opening can be checked, because the payload is no longer readable, while a retained salt would let anyone holding a candidate payload confirm a guess against $c\left({a}\right)$ ([Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s)). Destroying the salt does not weaken binding, which is a property of the commitment value: no second payload can be opened against $c\left({a}\right)$, and after ${t}^{I}\left({a}\right)$ no payload can be opened against it at all. A party that holds its own copy of the payload and must later prove that it corresponds to $c\left({a}\right)$ has to obtain and keep the opening before invalidation; the audit store does not keep one for it. The scheme must be hiding: an adversary holding $c\left({a}\right)$ and lacking $r\left({a}\right)$ must learn nothing about $p\left({a}\right)$. A bare unsalted hash of the payload does not satisfy this and must not be used, for the reason given in [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s).
*The invalidation registry.* Invalidation entries are appended to the audit trail as first-class records. Each entry $\iota \left({a}\right)$ contains the identifier of the invalidated record, the invalidation month, the legal ground, the authorising actor, and a commitment to the destroyed key’s identifier: not to the key itself. The registry is append-only. Invalidation is an event that is logged, not an event that erases the log. Key-management guidance anticipates exactly this record: once a key is destroyed, “its previous existence may be recorded (e.g., in metadata or audit logs)” (Barker, 2020, [Section 7.6](#bookmark=id.n9ol3kt5f9jg)). The invalidation entry is that record, given a legal ground and an authorising actor.
*Tamper evidence.* An append-only registry is only as good as the means of detecting an append-only violation. Secure audit logging has addressed this since Schneier and Kelsey (1999), whose hash-chained logs make earlier entries unalterable without detection; Merkle trees (Merkle, 1988) let the same assurance be checked for a single entry with a logarithmic proof (Crosby & Wallach, 2009), and Certificate Transparency standardised that construction for public logs (Laurie, Langley, & Kasper, 2013). The mechanism appends every access event, invalidation and subject-link removal to such a log, with the leaf and node hashing of RFC 6962, and Semantics II condition (i) is checked as an inclusion proof against the log’s root rather than as the presence of fields ([Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.7](#bookmark=id.2zhv84ggfra9)). What enters a leaf is chosen so that the log never needs erasing: the accessor fields, the creation month and the commitment, never the payload and never the subject fields. The tension that [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.4](#bookmark=id.3sdtdkmqwjlq) found unresolved in blockchain audit logging, an immutable trail facing an erasure right, therefore does not arise: what the right and the ceiling reach is held outside the log and destroyed there, and what the log holds is what accountability requires.
*Accumulator-based validity witnesses.* The set of currently valid (non-invalidated) records is maintained in a dynamic cryptographic accumulator supporting efficient revocation (Camenisch & Lysyanskaya, 2002). This provides an auditor with a succinct proof that a given record either is or is not currently valid, without the auditor enumerating the registry. The accumulator is an efficiency and verifiability layer, not a load-bearing component of the propositions: Proposition 2 holds if validity is established by linear scan of the registry, and the accumulator makes that check succinct. The accumulator is specified but not implemented in the artefact ([Section 6.1](#bookmark=id.9z1hawlqzw7w)). Dynamic accumulators of the Camenisch and Lysyanskaya type also require a trusted accumulator manager holding a trapdoor, which adds a trust assumption stated in [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s).
*The auditor’s view.* After invalidation, an external auditor examining record $a$ can establish four things. The access event occurred, with all its accountability attributes, which follows from $m\left({a}\right)$. A specific payload was bound to that event, which follows from $c\left({a}\right)$. The payload was invalidated, and the auditor can see when, on what legal ground, and by whom, from $\iota \left({a}\right)$. And the record’s current validity status is as claimed, which follows from the accumulator witness where that layer is used, and otherwise from a scan of the registry. Each of these entries is, moreover, in the log as first written, which follows from its inclusion proof against the published root. What the auditor cannot do is read the payload. This is the intended state, and it is the difference between this mechanism and the practitioner crypto-shredding pattern reviewed in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.4](#bookmark=id.3sdtdkmqwjlq): that pattern retains ciphertext and asserts that erasure occurred, whereas this mechanism produces a verifiable record of what was invalidated and under what authority.
*End of life at floor expiry.* The constraints of [Section 4.4](#bookmark=id.5c174keulio8) govern the record’s behaviour through its retention window, but the window ends, and the model would be incomplete if it said nothing about what follows. After $t=t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right)$, the last month of the closed window on which C1 is defined, the retention obligation lapses, and with it the necessity that justified retaining $m\left({a}\right)$ under Article 17(3)(b). Because the metadata contains the patient pseudonym and the actor identifier, it is personal data, and the storage-limitation principle of Article 5(1)(e) GDPR requires that it not be kept in identifiable form longer than the purpose demands. The mechanism therefore specifies a terminal transition. In the first month after the window, $t\left({a}\right)+F\left({a}\right)+1$, the record undergoes a second invalidation, in which the identifying fields of $m\left({a}\right)$ are destroyed, together with $k\left({a}\right)$, the salt $r\left({a}\right)$ and the ciphertext where no earlier invalidation removed them. What remains is a non-identifiable residue, being the event type, the document category, the outcome, and the commitment, which is sufficient for statistical and assurance purposes and insufficient to relate the record to any data subject. The terminal transition is itself logged, and the record’s final state is the only state in the mechanism that is intended to be anonymous rather than pseudonymous in the sense of [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s). Where a longer-running obligation applies to the same record (a national archival duty, or litigation hold) the terminal transition is deferred and the floor parameter $F\left({a}\right)$ is set to the longer period, which is the parameterisation the model already supports.
*Applying the mechanism to the two cases.* For the cross-border primary-use case, the mechanism operates at the audit repository of the National Contact Point, at the point where the ATNA audit record is written. For the Secure Processing Environment case, it operates at the environment’s access-logging boundary. The identifiable log required by Article 73(1)(e) is written with its activity content committed rather than retained in plaintext beyond the ceiling, and with its subject fields held apart from its accessor fields. At ${t}_{\pi }\left({a}\right)+6$ the payload key is destroyed and, for logs kept at patient-record granularity, the subject fields are removed. The environment then holds a log that identifies every person who accessed it, when and under which permit, as Article 73(1)(e) requires, and holds no electronic health data from that log, as Article 68(12) requires on the broad reading. Whether auditing “all processing operations” after the ceiling also needs the subject link is an interpretive question this thesis cannot settle; [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8), [Section 7.4](#bookmark=id.ds5sargxa3ne) puts it to the supervisory authority.
## **4.9 Residue Analysis**
Proposition 2 leaves a residue: $m\left({a}\right),c\left({a}\right),\iota \left({a}\right)$, the leaf hashes of the audit log and, where the optional layer is used, the accumulator state. The salt $r\left({a}\right)$, the key $k\left({a}\right)$ and the ciphertext of $p\left({a}\right)$ are destroyed at invalidation ([Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv)). Whether the mechanism is lawful depends on whether this residue sits on the correct side of the threshold at which data cease to be personal. This section performs that analysis, and it is included because [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya) identified its absence as the fourth gap in the literature.
*The threat.* Finck’s analysis for the European Parliament establishes that hashed or encrypted data likely remain personal data under GDPR so long as re-identification remains possible (Finck, 2019; Finck, 2018). Applied to this mechanism, the threat is direct: if $c\left({a}\right)$ is an unsalted hash of the payload, then an adversary who can guess candidate payloads can confirm a guess by recomputing the hash. For clinical documents drawn from a constrained space (a diagnosis code, a medication from a formulary) the guessing space may be small enough to make this practical. An unsalted commitment would therefore be a surviving item of personal data, and the mechanism would have relocated the erasure problem rather than solved it.
*The response.* This is why the hiding property is a requirement of the design and not an implementation preference. With a per-record salt $r\left({a}\right)$ of adequate length, confirming a guessed payload requires the salt; the commitment alone leaks nothing. Because the salt is destroyed with the key, no party can confirm a guessed payload against $c\left({a}\right)$ after invalidation unless it kept its own opening beforehand. What has been destroyed is both the ability to *recover* the payload, which depended on $k\left({a}\right)$, and the ability to confirm a guess about it from the audit store, which depended on $r\left({a}\right)$.
The audit log raises the same threat one level up, and the same response answers it. A leaf hash must outlive the record’s fields, since the root depends on it, and it is computed over the accessor fields and the commitment. After the terminal transition the commitment survives and the accessor fields do not; an adversary who can enumerate candidate accessors, a small set in any one environment, could then recompute the leaf and confirm which accessor it was. The specification therefore places a per-entry random nonce in every leaf, held with the record and destroyed at the terminal transition with the identifying fields, so that a surviving leaf hash confirms nothing.
