The artefact does not implement the terminal transition, and its leaves omit the nonce accordingly ([Section 6.1](#bookmark=id.9z1hawlqzw7w)).
*The limit.* The residue therefore does not meet the strict Norwegian anonymisation threshold. Datatilsynet’s guidance holds that encryption protects rather than anonymises, and that data remain personal while any key or linkage capable of re-identification is retained (Datatilsynet, 2015). By that standard the residue, which keeps metadata identifying the access event, is best characterised as pseudonymised rather than anonymous until the terminal transition. This thesis does not claim otherwise, and any claim that the mechanism achieves anonymisation would be false.
*Why the mechanism is nonetheless defensible.* The applicable legal test is not anonymisation but erasure. The European Data Protection Board’s Guidelines 02/2025 accept that where physical deletion is not technically possible, deleting the decryption key can render data unintelligible and so serve the erasure obligation. They maintain at the same time that encrypted and hashed data may remain personal data, and that the unintelligibility holds at least until the algorithm is broken (European Data Protection Board, 2026b). The requirement that the controller document the threat model under which the data are considered unrecoverable is not the Board’s formulation. It is Aikebaier’s (2026) interpretation, which connects a Destruction-IND security notion to the Board’s criterion, and it is adopted here as a design discipline rather than asserted as a regulatory requirement. The final version 2.0, adopted on 7 July 2026 after public consultation, sharpens rather than softens the constraint this places on the present mechanism: it confirms that both metadata and content may in principle constitute personal data, and that this may extend to encrypted and hashed data. The residue characterisation of this section is therefore the one the Board’s final position requires, and a thesis claiming anonymisation for that residue would now be contradicted by the guidance it relies upon. The design consequence is that the mechanism’s lawfulness rests on a documented threat model, which must state: the custody boundary within which key destruction occurs; the assumed adversary’s access to that boundary; the leakage assumptions for the hardware holding key material; and the algorithmic-break horizon over which the ciphertext’s confidentiality is assumed to hold. A mechanism deployed without that documentation would not satisfy the Board’s condition however sound its cryptography.
*The trust assumptions.* Because key destruction is attested rather than proven, the mechanism’s guarantees rest on a set of assumptions that a deploying institution must be willing to accept, and naming them is part of the documentation the Board’s condition requires.
The controller is trusted to execute destruction when the invalidation entry says it did, and to have had no copy of the key outside the custody boundary at that moment. The custody boundary itself, whether a hardware security module or an equivalent key-management service, is trusted not to retain recoverable key material after a destruction instruction, and not to leak it through side channels during its lifetime. The audit-trail operator is trusted not to remove or alter entries, which the append-only construction makes detectable but not impossible: an altered entry fails its inclusion proof, and a rewritten history is exposed by a consistency proof between an earlier root and the current one, provided earlier roots are published or countersigned (Laurie, Langley, & Kasper, 2013). The artefact implements inclusion proofs only. Where the optional accumulator layer is used, its manager is also trusted, since a party holding the accumulator trapdoor can forge validity witnesses. And the cryptographic assumption is that the commitment scheme remains binding and hiding, and the payload cipher remains unbroken, across the retention horizon.
What an external auditor can verify without any of this trust is bounded. The auditor can verify that the metadata is internally consistent, that an invalidation entry exists with its month, ground and authorising actor, and that the entry is bound into the append-only trail. The auditor can also verify that a commitment survives, to which a payload could be opened if one were produced. What the auditor cannot verify is that the key is gone. That gap is the difference between attestation and proof, and it closes only with hardware-backed or cryptographically certified deletion, which [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.3](#bookmark=id.wg2ajvtemzxy) treats as the boundary of this contribution.
*The residual cryptographic risk.* Over a ten-year floor, the algorithmic-break horizon is a live concern rather than a formality: anything retained for a decade must be assumed to face cryptanalytic capability that does not exist when it is written. Deleting the ciphertext at invalidation ([Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv)) removes this exposure for the store’s own copy, so what is retained long-term is metadata, the commitment and the invalidation entry. The risk is reduced, not eliminated. Copies the store cannot delete at once, such as backups, hold ciphertext until rotation removes them; a record with no invalidation event keeps its ciphertext until the terminal transition; and the commitment must stay hiding across the horizon, which is a requirement on the hash function rather than on a cipher. This is recorded as a limitation in [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) rather than resolved here.
## **4.10 Rival Designs and Proposition 4**
Six alternative designs are considered. Five are rejected for stated reasons; the sixth is accepted for the ceiling alone and bounded by Proposition 4.
*Rival 1: Rely on the Article 17(3)(b) exemption and retain in full.* This is the dissolution argument answered in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.3](#bookmark=id.8miqhq2ijj5t) and [Section 4.2](#bookmark=id.czwt0vfyycw5) above. It fails on the necessity boundary: the exemption protects retention that the legal obligation requires, and [Section 4.2](#bookmark=id.czwt0vfyycw5) established that the accountability purpose does not require payload accessibility. It fails additionally and decisively in the Secure Processing Environment case, where Article 68(12) admits no exemption parallel to Article 17(3)(b), so that Corollary 1.2’s infeasibility survives the argument entirely.
*Rival 2: Anonymise the audit record instead.* If the record were genuinely anonymised, Datatilsynet’s equation of anonymisation with deletion would discharge the erasure obligation (Datatilsynet, n.d.-b). But genuine anonymisation of a cross-border audit record destroys its accountability function: an audit trail that cannot identify which clinician accessed which patient’s record is not an audit trail, and Article 73(1)(e) requires the logs to be *identifiable* in terms. Anonymisation satisfies C2 and C3 by violating C1.
*Rival 3: Minimise the payload at capture, so that nothing needs erasing.* Recording less at the outset is good practice and is compatible with this mechanism; where a deployment can minimise, the mechanism has less to invalidate. For cross-border records it does not dissolve the problem, because the payload is put there by the standard rather than by the deployment: the IHE patient-discovery transaction requires the audit message to carry the query segment, name and birth time included ([Section 4.3](#bookmark=id.b04xy7a2dxno)). A deployment cannot minimise it away without departing from the profile. In the Secure Processing Environment case minimisation is a genuine alternative for the ceiling: a log kept at dataset granularity carries no subject fields and falls outside Article 68(12) on either reading, at the cost of patient-level traceability. The specification requires logs to identify the actor and to cover “access to electronic health data”, and requires logging to be “proportionate, risk-based, and technically feasible” and to “avoid unnecessary collection of detailed user behaviour not required for auditability or misuse detection” (TEHDAS2, 2026, Table 5.4, OPR-17, p. 51). It sets no requirement on the granularity of logs, which leaves the choice, and with it Corollary 1.2, to the operator. Minimisation does not remove from the scope of Article 17 the payload the standard requires, which is the case Proposition 4 below shows no relocation or reduction of the log can escape.
*Rival 4: Delete the record and log the deletion.* This is the closest rival and deserves the most care. Deleting the audit record while logging that a deletion occurred satisfies C2 and C3, and preserves a trace. It fails C1 under both semantics: under Semantics I trivially, and under Semantics II because condition (ii) fails: no commitment survives, so the auditor can establish that *something* was deleted but not that the deleted item was the payload bound to that specific access event. The distinction matters in adversarial conditions. A controller who deletes records and logs deletions can conceal the substitution of one record for another; a controller bound to a surviving commitment cannot.can conceal the substitution of one record for another. A commitment bound into the log at write time constrains this only for a party that kept its own opening; once the salt and payload are destroyed no auditor can open it, so the advantage over this rival is narrower than first stated. The mechanism’s advantage over Rival 4 is precisely the verifiability that [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya) identified as absent from the practitioner crypto-shredding pattern.
*Rival 5: Retain recoverable encrypted copies until the later date.* This is the resolution developed in the closest prior art, the DePaul retention-and-purging programme reviewed in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.4](#bookmark=id.3sdtdkmqwjlq). It holds encrypted copies in shadow tables and backups, with each copy’s key selected to expire on the governing purge date, and effects purging by destroying that key (Scope, Rasin, Lenard, Heart, & Wagner, 2022; Scope & Rasin, 2025). Where both obligations are floors and the purge date is fixed in advance, this is the right design.
It cannot work against a ceiling, and the reason is the residue analysis of [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s) applied in reverse. A copy whose key still exists is recoverable, and recoverable ciphertext held together with the means of decryption remains personal data under the threshold set out in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.3](#bookmark=id.8miqhq2ijj5t). Retaining such copies to satisfy the Article 73(1)(e) floor is therefore exactly what the Article 68(12) ceiling forbids of the environment holding them. The prior art satisfies a retention obligation by preserving recoverability; the mechanism specified here satisfies one by destroying recoverability and preserving accountability instead. That inversion, rather than any difference in cryptographic technique, is what the tri-lateral case requires.
*Rival 6: Move the logs out of the environment at permit closure.* If Article 68(12) is read by location, exporting the access logs at permit closure to an audit store outside the environment, held for instance by the health data access body, satisfies it literally without cryptography, on the premise that Article 73(1)(e) fixes how long the logs are kept and not where. The rival is correct about the ceiling, and this thesis accepts it as a sufficient answer to Corollary 1.2. It does not answer the erasure right, for a reason that is general enough to state as a result.
*Proposition 4 (location and right).* Let a ceiling be anchored to a location, requiring data to be absent from that location after a deadline, and let a right be anchored to the data subject, requiring data to be inaccessible to any controller holding them after a deadline. Under Semantics I, relocating a record before the ceiling’s deadline satisfies the ceiling and the floor together, while the floor and the right remain infeasible for every record satisfying the first disjunct of Proposition 1.
*Proof.* The ceiling quantifies over the location: after relocation the record is not in it, so the ceiling holds, and on the rival’s premise the floor is met at the new location. The right quantifies over the controller: Article 17(1) obliges the controller holding the data to erase them, and a controller receiving the record receives the obligation with itand, as a legal premise rather than a mathematical consequence, a controller receiving the record receives the obligation with it. Relocation therefore leaves C1 and C2 as they were, and the argument of Proposition 1 applies unchanged. ∎
Two consequences follow. Cryptographic invalidation is necessary for the request-driven conflict, which no relocation escapes, and optional for the location-anchored one, where relocation is a lawful alternative. And relocation is not free. The exported log still carries its subject fields, now held by a second controller for the rest of the floor, so the personal data have been moved rather than reduced; where those fields are electronic health data, they are held outside the measures Article 73(1) prescribes for such data. The partition of [Section 4.7](#bookmark=id.qemvcyvw7sy2) meets the ceiling without moving anything, and does so with the same mechanism that meets the right.
*The critique that is not a rival.* SecuPi (2025) argues that cryptographic erasure introduces operational complexity in row-level encryption scenarios and that auditable key management adds rather than removes overhead. This is not an alternative design for the problem; it is a cost objection, and it is partly correct. Per-record key granularity in a high-volume audit repository is an operational burden. The response is that the burden is the price of a solution to a problem that has none otherwise, and that the burden falls on audit records rather than on clinical data stores, which is the smaller of the two surfaces. [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) engages this critique at length rather than dismissing it.
## **4.11 Integration with the Norwegian Infrastructure**
The mechanism is specified against the Norwegian infrastructure as verified in [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.6](#bookmark=id.adz5cym51od1), not against an idealisation of it.
*Primary use: the National Contact Point.* Norway’s NCPeH is in live pilot operation (Helsedirektoratet, 2026), as [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.2](#bookmark=id.mfssrs4fkidd) describes. The mechanism attaches at the sixth step of the OpenNCP transmission flow, where the ATNA audit record is written to the audit repository. It requires no change to service discovery, patient discovery, document retrieval, pivot translation, or the security and consent module. This placement is deliberate: it is the narrowest point of the flow at which the intervention achieves its purpose, and interventions at the other five steps would touch the interoperability surface that Member States have agreed and Norway has implemented.
*Secondary use: Helsedataservice and the Secure Processing Environments.* Helsedataservice holds decision authority for eleven central health registries (Folkehelseinstituttet, 2024). The mechanism attaches at the access-logging boundary of the Secure Processing Environment rather than inside the environment’s analytical machinery. This placement is forced by the empirical finding that the Norwegian environment landscape is fragmented well beyond the three NORTRE nodes, extending to controller-provided servers, folders, and in some cases consumer cloud services and disconnected personal computers (SPUHiN, 2024). A mechanism requiring capabilities of the environment would fail against that reality; a mechanism operating on the log the environment must in any case produce does not. The reference architecture of the Joint Action’s specification locates the same boundary (TEHDAS2, 2026, Figure 5.13, p. 60). It divides a Secure Processing Environment into a control-and-management layer, comprising user authentication and identification, activity monitoring and access control, and the project workspaces in which data users work. The mechanism belongs to the activity-monitoring component, which writes the logs, and takes each permit’s expiry from the coordination portal of the health data access body, which issues the permit. It touches neither the project workspace nor the interfaces to data users and data holders.
*Compatibility with the national criteria.* The Norwegian criteria for Secure Processing Environments, in the version put to hearing, require an information-security management system as mandatory, recommend ISO 27001 certification, and require eID-based authentication at defined assurance levels (SPUHiN, 2025). The mechanism requires nothing beyond these: key custody within a documented boundary is an information-security-management concern of exactly the kind the mandatory requirement already covers. It adds no requirement that the criteria do not already impose, which was the design constraint derived from [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya)’s third gap.
*Relation to the pending implementing acts.* The binding technical requirements for Secure Processing Environments are to be laid down by Commission implementing acts under Article 73(5) EHDS, due by 26 March 2027 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025), after the submission of this thesis. The secondary-use provisions they will operationalise become applicable on 26 March 2029 under Article 105. The specification published by TEHDAS2 during 2026 as deliverable D7.4 is the best available anticipation of their content (TEHDAS2, 2026). The mechanism is therefore specified against a moving target, and the appropriate claim is compatibility with the infrastructure as currently specified rather than compliance with requirements not yet adopted. [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) treats the implications of this timing for the thesis’s policy relevance.
*Traceability.* [Table 4.1](#bookmark=id.ou2q52lu5vuw) sets the mechanism against each requirement it touches, so that the integration analysis above can be checked line by line rather than read as prose. ## **4.12 Summary**
This chapter formalised the tri-lateral retention conflict as a constraint-satisfaction problem over a single binary accessibility variable per record, with the retention floor parameterised so that the ten-year cross-border audit floor and the one-year Secure Processing Environment log floor are instances of one constraint. It proved that under plaintext-verifiability semantics the system is infeasible for any cross-border record whose erasure request arrives inside its window and, for Secure Processing Environment logs kept at patient-record granularity on the broad reading, without any erasure request at all, where two retention provisions of a single regulation collide over a single environment. It proved that under an accountability-preserving semantics the system is jointly satisfiable for every arrival pattern and every floor, and the proof exhibited the trajectory that achieves satisfaction. It showed that a ceiling collides with a floor only when it is no longer than the floor, and that the ceiling’s anchor decides whether the collision can be read from the text (Proposition 3), and that relocating a record meets the ceiling but not the right (Proposition 4). That trajectory, specified as Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation, retains metadata and a hiding commitment, and destroys the payload key at the earlier of the erasure deadline and the deletion ceiling. It appends the invalidation to a tamper-evident audit log as a first-class, witnessed event, in a log built never to hold what erasure reaches. The salt and the payload ciphertext go with the key. <comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4fE>At floor expiry it performs a terminal transition<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4fE> that destroys the identifying metadata, leaving a non-identifiable statistical residue, so that the record’s whole life cycle, not merely its retention window, is accounted for under the storage-limitation principle.
The mechanism’s residue is pseudonymised rather than anonymous by the strict Norwegian standard, it is defensible under the erasure test the European Data Protection Board has articulated provided the threat model is documented, and its long-horizon cryptographic risk is real and recorded. The limitations bearing on this chapter, the informal proof standard and the conditionality on honest key destruction among them, are those stated canonically in [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) and are not restated here. Six rival designs were considered: five were rejected on stated grounds and one, relocation, was accepted for the ceiling alone. The principal cost objection was acknowledged rather than dismissed. The integration analysis placed the mechanism at the two narrowest points of the Norwegian infrastructure at which it achieves its purpose, requiring nothing of the substrate that the national criteria do not already require.
[Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) demonstrates Propositions 1 and 2 executably, over synthetic records generated as described in Chapter 3.
# **Chapter 5. Demonstration**
*Every figure reported in this chapter was produced by the code listed in Appendix A, executed under seed 20260915. The full-cohort comparison of *[*Table 5.7*](#bookmark=id.tcfe3n4cqbml)* was recorded on 28 September with the code of that date; the committed-subset run (Appendix A, A.21) repeats it with the current code and gives the same figures.*
## **5.1 Purpose and Claim**
This chapter discharges Activity 4 of the design science cycle set out in [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.2](#bookmark=id.y6jetl7tk1p1): demonstration. Its function is narrow.
The chapter demonstrates that Propositions 1 and 2 of [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) hold on the instances examined; Propositions 3 and 4 are analytic and are not executed here, although [Section 5.4](#bookmark=id.dsdf4i82wfw7) computes the condition of Proposition 3. It does not verify them in the proof-assistant sense, it does not measure performance, and it does not deploy anything. Proposition 1 predicts that under plaintext-verifiability semantics the constraint system fails whenever an erasure deadline or a deletion-ceiling deadline falls inside a record’s retention window. Proposition 2 predicts that under accountability-preserving semantics the invalidation trajectory satisfies all three constraints for every arrival pattern. The demonstration’s job is to make both predictions checkable by execution rather than only by argument.
A subsidiary claim is made for Corollary 1.2: that, on the broad reading of Article 68(12) and for logs kept at patient-record granularity, Secure Processing Environment access-log records become infeasible under plaintext semantics *without any erasure request at all*, through the collision of the Article 73(1)(e) one-year retention floor with the Article 68(12) six-month deletion ceiling. The demonstration produces thirty-nine such witnesses.

  - *Secure Processing Environment access-log records*, F = 12 months, secondary pathway. Each carries a permit expiry at a uniformly distributed one to twelve months after creation. Erasure requests arrive with probability 0.25.

Under plaintext-verifiability semantics, $V\left({a,t}\right)=\alpha \left({a,t}\right)$, so constraint C1 requires the payload to remain accessible throughout the retention window while C2 and C3 require it to become inaccessible from their respective deadlines. The checker reports every month at which both are required at once.

The two counts differ because five SPE records collide with both C2 and C3; each is counted once in the per-record column and twice in the violation total. First, the violation rate is not one hundred per cent, and this is the correct behaviour. The rates in this chapter are functions of the generator parameters in [Table 5.2](#bookmark=id.jgvipiqoop1z) and are not estimates of real frequency; in particular, the generator treats every erasure request as valid, whereas many would be lawfully refused under Article 17(3) ([Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2)). A cross-border record for which no data subject ever exercises Article 17 has no second constraint to collide with C1, and is trivially feasible. The single exception is the record whose request arrived beyond the window, which is precisely the case the proposition excludes. The checker therefore reproduces the proposition’s conditional structure exactly, including its boundary.

## **5.4 Corollary 1.2: Infeasibility Without an Erasure Request**
Seventy-eight of the one hundred Secure Processing Environment records received no erasure request. Under the received account of the retention–erasure problem, these records should be unproblematic: no data subject has asked for anything, so there is nothing for the retention obligation to conflict with.
*<comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4ek>Thirty-nine of them are infeasible under Semantics I.<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4ek> That is exactly half of the records with no erasure request.*
The witnesses, verbatim:
rid=100: t\_a=7 permit expires t\_pi=10 -\> C3 from t=16, C1 to t=19  | collision at t=16
rid=103: t\_a=7 permit expires t\_pi=10 -\> C3 from t=16, C1 to t=19  | collision at t=16
rid=104: t\_a=3 permit expires t\_pi=4 -\> C3 from t=10, C1 to t=15  | collision at t=10
Take the first. The access-log record is created in month seven. Article 73(1)(e) requires the identifiable log to remain verifiable until month nineteen. The data permit expires in month ten, so Article 68(12) requires the electronic health data to be gone from the environment by month sixteen. Months sixteen through nineteen are therefore months in which the same regulation requires the same environment both to retain an identifiable access log and, if that log’s entries are themselves electronic health data, to hold none of them. No data subject has exercised any right. No deployment baseline is involved. No synthesis across instruments of differing legal weight has occurred. On the broad reading of Article 68(12), and for logs kept at patient-record granularity ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb)), the conflict is internal to Regulation (EU) 2025/327. Under the narrower reading, these thirty-nine witnesses lapse and the secondary-use collisions reduce to the nine records in this population whose erasure requests fall inside the retention window (four that collide with C2 only and five that also collide with C3; twenty-two records received requests in all); Proposition 1, Corollary 1.1, and every Semantics II result are unaffected. Moving the logs out of the environment at permit closure would also remove these thirty-nine collisions, at the cost set out in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.10](#bookmark=id.2c8thzi7kbd9); it would not remove the erasure-driven ones.
The fifty per cent figure follows from the generator. The collision occurs when ${t}_{\pi }+6\leq {t}_{a}+12$, the condition of Proposition 3(ii) with $F=12$, $L=6$ and the ceiling anchored to permit expiry, and permit lengths were drawn uniformly from one to twelve months, so half fall at or below six. A longer horizon lowers the rate as $6/{\pi }_{max}$ without removing the collision, which Proposition 1 establishes independently of any distribution.

## **5.8 What the Demonstration Establishes, and What It Does Not**
*Established.* Both propositions hold on all two hundred generated instances. Proposition 1’s conditional structure is reproduced exactly, including the boundary case of the request falling outside the window. Corollary 1.2 has thirty-nine witnesses in the model: records in which two provisions of one regulation collide over one environment with no data-subject action involved. The infeasibility results survive a separately written exhaustive search that considers every possible accessibility assignment rather than only the trajectory the main checker examines. The invalidation trajectory eliminates every violation without introducing any.
*Not established, and not claimed.* The demonstration does not prove the propositions for all instances; it checks them on the instances generated under one seed, and the exhaustive cross-check covers four small cases rather than the general result. The proofs in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), not this chapter, carry the general claim. No performance measurement was taken, and no statement about execution time, throughput, or storage overhead appears anywhere in this thesis. The sandbox does not connect to any National Contact Point, implement the OpenNCP transmission flow, or evaluate consent policies. Key destruction is simulated by removing a reference in program state, which demonstrates the mechanism’s logic and demonstrates nothing whatever about whether key destruction can be assured in deployment. An optional module repeats the lifecycle with real AES-256-GCM envelope encryption (Appendix A, A.15 and A.22): after the 138 scheduled destructions exactly those records refuse to decrypt and the other 62 still read, so unreadability is executed rather than asserted; the keys are still destroyed in program memory, not in hardware: the limitation that [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya) drew from the secure-deletion literature and that [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal) engages.
