# **Chapter 6. Discussion**
## **6.1 What the Thesis Establishes**
The thesis establishes that the conflict between audit-retention floors and the obligations to erase is not a property of the obligations but of an assumption about what satisfies them. Under plaintext-verifiability semantics, a record is verifiable while its payload is readable, and the constraint system has no solution for any record whose erasure deadline falls inside its retention window. Under a semantics in which a record is verifiable while its accountability content is intact and any loss of payload accessibility is itself logged, grounded, and attributed, the system is satisfiable for every arrival pattern of erasure requests and permit expiries, and for every retention floor. [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) proves both results; [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) witnesses them executably, and a separately written exhaustive search confirms that under the first semantics no assignment of payload accessibility whatsoever could succeed.
The request-driven form of the conflict cannot be escaped by moving the record. A deletion ceiling anchored to a location yields to relocation, but the right to erasure attaches to whichever controller holds the data ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.10](#bookmark=id.2c8thzi7kbd9), Proposition 4). Cryptographic invalidation is therefore necessary where a data subject’s request meets a retention floor, and in the cross-border pathway that is every request arriving inside the floor, because the patient-discovery transaction puts the patient’s identifying query into the audit record by design.
The sharpest instance is narrower, and rests on one contestable interpretive step. Article 73(1)(e) requires identifiable logs of access to and activity in a Secure Processing Environment to be kept for at least one year. Article 68(12) requires “the electronic health data within the secure processing environment” to be deleted within six months of the expiry of the data permit. Where an environment logs access at patient-record granularity, those log entries are electronic health data within the environment on the broad reading, and where the remaining permit duration at the time a log is written is six months or less, the two requirements overlap with no data subject acting. [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb) sets out the grounds on both sides. [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) produced thirty-nine witnesses of this collision in the model, in a population of one hundred Secure Processing Environment records; across the full population of two hundred, cross-border records included, ninety records were infeasible under Semantics I, most of them through erasure requests ([Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Table 5.3](#bookmark=id.a33vq5enjafd)). Proposition 3 states the general condition: a ceiling no longer than the floor, anchored to an event other than the one the floor runs from. On the narrow reading, or where logs are kept at dataset granularity, the collision does not arise. On either reading the mechanism meets both provisions, because the accessor fields that Article 73(1)(e) requires to be identifiable are not the subject fields that Article 68(12) may reach.
Finally, the thesis specifies the mechanism that the feasibility proof exhibits: per-record keys under a key-encrypting key, hiding commitments, deletion of the ciphertext with the key, removal of the subject link at the ceiling, invalidation entries carrying month, legal ground, and authorising actor, a tamper-evident log built never to hold what erasure reaches, and a terminal transition at floor expiry that discharges the storage-limitation obligation on the metadata itself. The artefact executes all of these but the terminal transition, which [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv) specifies and the checker does not implement; nor does it implement the per-entry nonce that keeps surviving leaf hashes from confirming guesses ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s)). The specification also provides for accumulator-based validity witnesses, which are an efficiency and verifiability layer rather than a component of either proposition, since Proposition 2 holds if validity is established by linear scan. They are specified but not implemented: the demonstration of [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1) exercises keys, commitments, and invalidation entries, and no accumulator was built or run.
What follows engages the objections to all of this in the order of their seriousness.
## **6.2 The Authority Problem**
The most serious objection to this thesis is not technical. It is that Semantics II is an argument, not an authority.
No regulator, court, or supervisory authority has held that an audit record whose payload has been cryptographically invalidated continues to satisfy a retention obligation. The thesis argues that it does. Article 17(3)(b) protects only processing that is *necessary* for the legal obligation, and Article 5(1)(c) requires that no more personal data be retained than the purpose demands. The accountability purpose of an audit record is served by knowing who accessed what, when, and under what authority, not by continued readability of the clinical payload. The Norwegian Data Protection Authority’s internal-control guidance places exactly this balancing on the controller (Datatilsynet, n.d.-a), and its privacy-by-design guidance equates anonymisation with deletion (Datatilsynet, n.d.-b). But none of this amounts to a holding that invalidation discharges retention.
If a supervisory authority takes the view that Article 73(1)(e)’s requirement of “identifiable logs” entails logs whose subject matter remains readable, then Proposition 2 remains mathematically true and becomes practically inert: the mechanism would satisfy a constraint system that does not describe the law. The thesis would still have established the collision, which is textual and, on the narrow reading of Article 68(12), survives in its erasure-driven form, and would still have established that the collision is *dissolvable in principle* by a semantic move. It would not have established that the move is available.
Three considerations bear on how likely that outcome is, and they are offered as reasons rather than reassurance.
First, the alternative readings are worse. If verifiability requires readability, then on the broad reading the only way to honour both Article 73(1)(e) and Article 68(12) is to move the logs out of the environment at permit closure ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.10](#bookmark=id.2c8thzi7kbd9), Rival 6): the subject fields then sit with a second controller for the rest of the floor, and the erasure right is untouched (Proposition 4). For cross-border records there is no such route at all. A supervisory authority is unlikely to prefer that outcome to a reading under which every obligation is honoured where the data are.
Second, the direction of regulatory travel favours the argument. The European Data Protection Board’s Guidelines 02/2025 were finalised as version 2.0 on 7 July 2026. They accept that where physical deletion is not technically possible, deleting the decryption key can render the data unintelligible and so serve the erasure obligation, while maintaining that encrypted and hashed data may themselves remain personal data and that the unintelligibility holds at least until the algorithm is broken (European Data Protection Board, 2026b). The further qualification that such a substitution depends on a *documented threat model* is not the Board’s formulation but Aikebaier’s (2026), whose equivalence proposition connects a Destruction-IND security notion to the Board’s criterion; the distinction is preserved here because the two carry different authority. What the Guidelines themselves supply is a functional rather than literal reading of an obligation: the same move Semantics II makes on the retention side. The Joint Action’s specification points the same way from the infrastructure side. It requires deletion at permit expiry “while ensuring compliance with applicable legal obligations and traceability or reproducibility requirements” and leaves the deletion and retention policy to “balance these obligations” (TEHDAS2, 2026, Table 5.2, OPR-6, p. 43), and it records that further guidance is needed on how accountability and anonymisation obligations intersect (Annex 7, p. 96). A specification that asks for a balance it does not define has not adopted plaintext verifiability; [Table 4.1](#bookmark=id.ou2q52lu5vuw) sets out one balance requirement by requirement.
Third, the question is decidable by asking. [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8) proposes, as the highest-value next step, seeking an opinion on whether accountability-preserving verifiability discharges the retention obligation in Article 73(1)(e). Datatilsynet is the natural addressee for the GDPR-side questions; because Articles 68 and 73 are provisions of the EHDS Regulation, the Norwegian authorities responsible for its incorporation (Helsedirektoratet and the Ministry of Health and Care Services) and the Commission are the more appropriate addressees for those. That is a tractable request with a determinate answer, and it would convert the thesis’s central interpretive move from argument to authority or else refute it cleanly. Either outcome is worth more than the present uncertainty.
A second authority question sits beside the first and is narrower. Whether Article 68(12) reaches the access logs is a question of statutory construction that a supervisory authority or, ultimately, a court will settle, and that this author cannot. The thesis states Corollary 1.2 conditionally rather than adopting the broad reading or the narrow one, on the grounds set out in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb). What makes this tolerable rather than fatal is that the dependency is confined: Corollary 1.2 stands or falls with it, and nothing else in the thesis does. The same request, addressed to the authorities responsible for EHDS incorporation, could reasonably carry this one alongside it.
## **6.3 Key Destruction and the Limits of Assurance**
The second objection is the one the thesis has carried since [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), and it is the ceiling of the contribution.
The mechanism’s guarantees are conditional on the irreversible destruction of key material. The canonical systematisation of secure deletion establishes that the further a deletion approach operates from the physical storage medium, the harder it becomes to assert that destruction actually occurred (Reardon, Basin, & Capkun, 2013). Cryptographic erasure is the limiting case: it operates entirely above the medium, reducing the deletion of arbitrary data to the deletion of a key, and inheriting in concentrated form the problem that key destruction cannot be confirmed by inspection.
The thesis’s response is to be precise about what the invalidation entry is. It is an *attested* record of destruction, not a *proof* of it. The entry records that a named actor destroyed a named key at a named month on a named legal ground, and binds that claim into an append-only Merkle log alongside a commitment to the destroyed key’s identifier, so that the claim, once made, cannot be altered or withdrawn without detection ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv)). Key-management guidance treats such a record as the normal trace of a destroyed key (Barker, 2020). An auditor can establish that the claim was made, by whom, and when; an auditor cannot establish that the claim is true. The difference between attestation and proof is the boundary of this contribution. Two things narrow it without closing it. Hardware security modules validated against FIPS 140-3 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2019) place destruction inside a tested boundary, though validation attests the design of the module, not any particular destruction. And the optional module of the artefact replaces the simulated key with real AES-256-GCM envelope encryption: after the 138 scheduled destructions, exactly those records refuse to decrypt ([Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.8](#bookmark=id.nkz790ri7jg7)), which shows that unreadability follows from the destruction, not that the destruction took place.
That boundary is where an active research programme sits. Proof-of-secure-erasure protocols seek evidence that a prover has erased its memory, with recent work relaxing the isolation assumptions such protocols traditionally require (Bursuc, Gil-Pons, Mauw, & Trujillo-Rasua, 2024). In the quantum setting, encryption with certified deletion produces a deletion certificate, and its authors identify *public verifiability*, enabling parties other than the originator to verify such a certificate, as an open problem (Broadbent & Islam, 2020). Were public verifiability of deletion certificates achieved, the invalidation entry specified in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) could carry a proof rather than an attestation, and the mechanism’s guarantee would strengthen from conditional to demonstrable without any change to the model.
One further consideration limits the practical weight of this objection. The alternative to attested key destruction is not proven deletion; it is unattested deletion. A controller who deletes an audit record and logs that a deletion occurred is making exactly the same kind of unverifiable claim, with strictly less structure: there is no surviving commitment, so an auditor cannot even establish *what* was destroyed. The mechanism does not solve the assurance problem. It does improve on every available alternative with respect to it.
## **6.4 The Cost Objection**
SecuPi (2025) argues that cryptographic erasure introduces operational complexity in row-level encryption scenarios, that auditable key management adds rather than removes overhead, and that policy-based access control is a better answer to the right to erasure in heavily distributed systems. This critique is substantially correct on its own terms and must be engaged rather than dismissed.
The mechanism specified in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) requires per-record key granularity, and [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv) explains why: invalidation events occur at record granularity, because a permit expiry invalidates the records of one permit while an erasure request invalidates the records relating to one data subject, and those sets intersect without nesting. Coarser granularity would make some invalidations impossible to perform without over-invalidating. Per-record keys in a high-volume audit repository are an operational burden, and the thesis does not pretend otherwise.
Three observations bound that burden without denying it.
The burden falls on audit records rather than on clinical data stores. The mechanism operates at the audit-trail boundary (the sixth step of the MyHealth@EU transmission flow, or the access-logging boundary of a Secure Processing Environment) not on the electronic health records themselves. This is the smaller of the two surfaces by a wide margin, and the placement was chosen for that reason as much as for substrate independence.
The burden is bounded and auditable in a way the alternative’s is not. Key-management overhead is a known quantity that scales with record volume and can be budgeted, monitored, and inspected. The residual-copy problem that plaintext deletion faces (establishing that no backup, cache, replica, or derived index retains the deleted data) is unbounded and largely uninspectable. Trading an unbounded and invisible cost for a bounded and visible one is a defensible engineering choice, and it is the choice the mechanism makes.
The critique’s proposed alternative does not address the problem this thesis identifies. Policy-based and attribute-based access control govern *who may read* data; they do not cause data to cease to be readable. Against Article 68(12), which requires that electronic health data not remain in the environment, an access-control answer does not satisfy the obligation: the data remain, protected by policy. Against the collision of Corollary 1.2, access control offers nothing at all. The critique is well-aimed at crypto-shredding as a general answer to the right to erasure, which is the claim SecuPi is addressing; it is not aimed at the tri-lateral retention problem, and does not reach it.
## **6.5 Scalability**
The demonstration ran two hundred records. A national audit repository handles volumes several orders of magnitude larger, and the mechanism’s costs do not all scale in the same way.
Three components grow linearly with the number of records and present no difficulty at realistic volumes, and the audit log adds a fourth whose verification grows only logarithmically: an inclusion proof for one entry in a log of $n$ entries needs about ${log}_{2}n$ hashes, some thirty for a billion entries, which is why the same construction carries the web’s certificate logs (Laurie, Langley, & Kasper, 2013). Metadata and commitments are small fixed-size additions per record; the invalidation registry grows only with the number of invalidation events, which is bounded by the number of records but in practice far smaller; and the feasibility check itself is a per-record operation independent of the rest of the population.
The key registry is where the cost concentrates, and it is the component the cost objection of [Section 6.4](#bookmark=id.6dcjhrktbx5i) correctly identifies. Per-record keys mean one key-management entry per audit record, and at national cross-border volumes over a ten-year retention horizon that is a large registry to maintain, back up, and audit. Two properties mitigate the growth without eliminating it. Keys for invalidated records are destroyed rather than retained, so the live registry shrinks as invalidations accumulate, and over a long horizon the steady-state registry is smaller than the cumulative record count. And key material is small and uniform, so the registry is an indexing and custody problem rather than a storage one.
The accumulator layer has the least favourable scaling profile and is also the most dispensable. Dynamic accumulators with efficient revocation require witness maintenance as the accumulated set changes, and witness update costs grow with the frequency of revocation. This is why [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv) specifies the accumulator as a verifiability and efficiency layer rather than a component of either proposition: an implementation that finds witness maintenance too costly at its volume can establish validity by scanning the invalidation registry, losing succinctness and retaining correctness. The Merkle log already makes the presence of an invalidation entry succinct to check; what the accumulator would add is a succinct proof that a record has *not* been invalidated.
No measurement supports any of this. The demonstration made no performance claim and none is made here; these are structural observations about how the specified components grow, and establishing their practical limits is work for an implementation rather than for this thesis.
## **6.6 Evaluation Design and the Role of Stakeholder Assessment**
The evaluation reported in this thesis is analytical, and [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2) states its criteria. That evaluation assesses whether the artefact is internally coherent, whether it fits the infrastructure it was designed against, and whether its results reproduce. It does not assess whether the people who would have to deploy it find it defensible, implementable, or trustworthy, and those are different questions that analytical evaluation cannot answer.
An instrument for answering them has been designed and is specified in full in Appendix C. It comprises an eight-person expert panel spanning data protection, health IT architecture, Secure Processing Environment operation, and information logistics, and a session structure in which participants describe current practice before being shown the mechanism. It also comprises a demonstration script that runs the artefact and states its limitations before participants are invited to find them, a semi-structured interview guide, and a sixteen-item closed-response instrument across perceived utility, regulatory alignment, operational viability, and audit integrity.
Three questions in that instrument bear directly on matters this chapter has had to leave open, and the connection is worth making explicit. Interview question seven asks practitioners whether Article 68(12) reaches the access logs an environment generates, which is the interpretive condition [Section 6.2](#bookmark=id.51bwj2518vrs) identifies as carrying Corollary 1.2. Questionnaire item A2 asks whether attested key destruction is sufficient without hardware-backed proof, which is the boundary [Section 6.3](#bookmark=id.wg2ajvtemzxy) describes. And items O1 to O4 address the operational burden that [Section 6.4](#bookmark=id.6dcjhrktbx5i) concedes and cannot quantify. Each of these is a question about practitioner judgement rather than about the model, and none can be settled by further analysis.
The instrument has not been executed, for the reasons given in [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.8](#bookmark=id.7zb7sm2heax): doing so would process personal data about identifiable professionals, require notification to Sikt, and require revision of the scope and ethics statements that are accurate for the thesis as submitted. Its execution is the immediate next step identified in [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8), [Section 7.5](#bookmark=id.clphjrvscppc), and the findings would feed back into the design cycle rather than being appended to it, revising the trust model of [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s), the residue analysis, and the direction of the next iteration.
## **6.7 Synthetic Data and the Limits of the Demonstration**
Substituting real FHIR R4 resources for constructed payload strings changed all two hundred commitments and no reported figure ([Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.8](#bookmark=id.nkz790ri7jg7), [Table 5.7](#bookmark=id.tcfe3n4cqbml)), as it must, since no constraint in the TRF Model reads payload content.
The two limitations of the generated cohort, US Core rather than Norwegian profiles and the validity bounds found by Chen, Chun, Patel, Chiang and James (2019), are stated in [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.5](#bookmark=id.xq8ezeyqxwsd); both lie in dimensions the thesis does not use, because its claims concern the behaviour of audit records under constraint, not clinical content.
The deeper limitation is that a demonstration over generated instances is not a proof over all instances. The general claims rest on the arguments in [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), and those arguments are informal rather than machine-checked. The executable check and the exhaustive cross-check reduce the probability that an error in the proofs has gone unnoticed; they do not eliminate it.
## **6.8 Implications for Practice and Policy**
The timing argument is the strongest claim to practical relevance this thesis makes.
Regulation (EU) 2025/327 entered into force on 26 March 2025. Under Article 105 it applies generally from 26 March 2027, and the secondary-use provisions of Chapter IV, which contain both Article 68(12) and Article 73(1)(e), apply from 26 March 2029. Article 73(5) requires the Commission, by means of implementing acts and by 26 March 2027, to lay down the technical, organisational, information-security, confidentiality, data-protection, and interoperability requirements for Secure Processing Environments.
The collision this thesis characterises is therefore not yet operative, and the specifications that will determine how it is handled are not yet written. That is an unusually favourable position for a piece of academic work to occupy. A framework that arrives after infrastructure has hardened around a problem is archaeology; one that arrives while the specifications are being drafted can affect defaults. The Norwegian position sharpens this further: the national criteria for Secure Processing Environments went through a public hearing in the SPUHiN process from July to October 2025, and are positioned explicitly as a national reference basis pending the Union implementing act (SPUHiN, 2025). The compliance checklists, in the hearing version inspected, address information-security management, identity assurance, and access governance. They grade an information-security management system as mandatory and ISO 27001 certification as recommended, and require eID-based authentication at defined assurance levels. No requirement addressing the reconciliation of retention with erasure and deletion appears among them. The absence is observed in the hearing version of the checklists, not established against the deliverable as submitted.
The state of Norwegian cross-border operations reinforces this. Norway’s National Contact Point is in live pilot operation, but no relevant patients had yet presented when the Directorate last reported (Helsedirektoratet, 2026), as [Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.2](#bookmark=id.mfssrs4fkidd) sets out. The cross-border audit stream has effectively not begun. A design element proposed now would shape how those records are structured from the outset rather than requiring their retrospective reconstruction.
Three concrete implications follow for the bodies that will write the specifications.
For the Commission drafting the Article 73(5) implementing acts, the reconciliation of Article 73(1)(e) with Article 68(12) is a question the acts must answer, and this thesis offers a candidate answer that does not require amending either provision. Proposition 3 also gives the acts a drafting test: any further ceiling no longer than a floor and anchored to a different event will collide for some records, and only the records’ histories will show which. Silence in the implementing acts would leave every Health Data Access Body to resolve the collision independently, which is the outcome that produces the fragmentation the EHDS exists to prevent.
For Health Data Access Bodies including Helsedataservice, the invalidation entry is the practical takeaway even if the full mechanism is not adopted: recording *what was invalidated, when, on what legal ground, and by whom* as a first-class audit event costs little and converts an unexplained absence into an accountable one.
For TEHDAS2 and its successors, whose Secure Processing Environment specification of 2026 defines minimum capabilities and the interoperability baseline for federating environments, the collision is named but not resolved: the specification asks for a balance between deletion and traceability and flags the intersection of accountability and anonymisation as needing guidance ([Section 6.2](#bookmark=id.51bwj2518vrs)). [Table 4.1](#bookmark=id.ou2q52lu5vuw) is written in the specification’s own requirement identifiers so that it can be read as a proposal against them.
This thesis is a Master’s dissertation proposing a design, not a regulatory impact assessment. The policy implications above are offered as an argument to the bodies concerned, not as advice they are obliged to weigh, and their force depends entirely on the authority question of [Section 6.2](#bookmark=id.51bwj2518vrs) being resolved favourably.
## **6.9 Theoretical Implications**
Three contributions to the scholarly conversation follow from the work, each modest and each stated at its actual size.
The first is the formalisation itself. Treating a retention conflict as a constraint-satisfaction problem over a single binary accessibility variable per record, and making the semantics of verifiability an explicit parameter of the model rather than an unexamined assumption, is a way of stating retention problems that appears not to have been used before in this domain. The general method of formalising legal compliance as satisfiability is established (Feng, Marsso, Sabetzadeh, & Chechik, 2023); its application here is what is new, and the applicability of the formulation beyond health data is an open question the thesis does not settle. The structure (one or more floors, a subject-triggered right, a ceiling) is not obviously specific to health. [Section 6.10](#bookmark=id.odezbdc5356l) tests that expectation against a statute outside health and returns a negative result which revises it: what matters is not that a floor and a ceiling coexist but where the ceiling is anchored.
The second is the identification of the semantic assumption as the locus of the problem. The literature treats the retention-erasure tension as a conflict between obligations. The model locates it instead in an interpretive assumption that neither obligation states, and shows that the assumption is doing the work: with it, infeasibility; without it, satisfiability. This reframing suggests a general question for regulatory-compliance modelling, namely how many apparent conflicts between legal obligations are artefacts of implicit operational semantics inherited from systems built under earlier law.
The third is the positioning of the contribution relative to the cryptographic literature. Aikebaier’s (2026) systematisation of cryptographic erasure closes by naming five open problems, of which the fifth is erasure under multi-regime retention conflict. That source is an unreviewed preprint and is cited as corroboration rather than authority. This thesis addresses the problem in one regulatory setting, with the reservations of [Sections 6.2](#bookmark=id.51bwj2518vrs) and 6.3 attached. The fourth open problem on the same list, composition with zero-knowledge selective disclosure, is a problem this thesis creates rather than solves, and [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8) treats it accordingly.
## **6.10 Where the Ceiling Is Anchored: a Cross-Sector Test**
The first of those three contributions raised a question it did not answer. If the structure of one or more floors, a subject-triggered right and a ceiling is not specific to health, then some other domain ought to exhibit it, and running that domain through the same model ought to produce the same infeasibility. A cross-sector instance was therefore constructed and executed rather than argued.
The instance is Norwegian police register law. Section 17 of politiregisterloven imposes a traceability duty on the use of police information systems and converts it into a retention rule: *Opplysninger om bruk av systemet skal registreres og lagres i minst 1 år og slettes senest etter 3 år* (Politiregisterloven, 2010, § 17). The provision therefore places a floor of twelve months and a ceiling of thirty-six months on the same access log, outside health, and the data subject’s rights operate on that log as they do on any other personal data. On the reading that motivated the thesis, this ought to be a second instance of the tri-lateral collision.
It is not, and the result is the more informative one. Sixty records were generated under a floor of twelve months and a ceiling of thirty-six, with erasure requests arriving as they do elsewhere in the demonstration. Seven records carried at least one Semantics I violation. Of those seven, **none** arose without an erasure request. Under Semantics II there were no violations at all, and every record was invalidated at its scheduled month. The module that produces this is listed in full at Appendix A, Section A.13, and its console output at Section A.20.
The zero is the finding. <comment_start id=AAACH_Ls4e4>Section 17 fixes both of its limbs<comment_end id=AAACH_Ls4e4> against the same event, the making of the log entry: the log is stored for at least a year from that point and deleted at the latest three years from the same point. Two periods measured from one origin, the later longer than the earlier, do not collide; they bound a retention window, and the later limit is simply the end of it. Every collision the model finds in this instance is therefore erasure-driven, which is the ordinary bi-lateral conflict the literature already describes, not the structure this thesis is about.
Article 68(12) behaves differently for a structural reason as well as a numerical one: its ceiling is shorter than the floor, which any collision requires, and it is anchored where the shortfall cannot be seen. Its ceiling is anchored not to the creation of the record but to the expiry of the data permit, an event external to the record and capable of falling at any point relative to the floor, including before the floor has run. A floor measured from creation and a ceiling measured from an unrelated later event are not two ends of one window; they are two clocks that can cross. That crossing is what Proposition 1 characterises, Corollary 1.2 is the case where it happens with no erasure request present at all, and [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb) states the general condition as Proposition 3: floor and ceiling collide for a record exactly when the ceiling’s end falls inside the floor, which needs a ceiling no longer than the floor and, under an external anchor, depends on each record’s history.
This sharpens the contribution and narrows it at the same time. It suggests that the diagnostic question for any candidate instance is not whether a floor and a ceiling both exist, which is common, but whether a ceiling no longer than the floor is anchored to a different event, which is not ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), Proposition 3). It also withdraws the loose expectation, expressed in the preceding section, that any domain combining the three constraint types will exhibit the collision. Financial record-keeping under MiFID II remains a candidate on that revised test only if some ceiling there is anchored externally, which this thesis has not investigated.
Three limits belong with the result. The instance is illustrative and not empirical: no Norwegian police data was obtained, no operational retention practice was observed, and the record population was generated exactly as elsewhere in the demonstration. The provision does not state in words when either period begins; that both run from the log entry is a reading of the sentence’s own syntax, and a reader who requires the anchor to be expressly fixed will find that Section 17 does not fix it. And whether the mechanism of [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) transfers to a record-level ceiling in a policing context is a design question this thesis does not open. What the instance establishes is narrower and sufficient: that the collision at the centre of this thesis depends on where a ceiling is anchored, and that a statute pairing a floor with a longer ceiling from a single origin does not produce it.
## **6.11 Boundaries as Contribution**
The thesis makes one bounded claim and prices every limitation into it in advance. The proofs are informal, not machine-checked. The demonstration covers generated instances under one seed, not all instances. Key destruction is simulated in program state and says nothing about deployment assurance. The synthetic records carry US Core profiles, not Norwegian ones. The cryptographic primitives are established technique, not novel construction. The closest prior art is a patent claiming key-expiry selection for retention-purge conflicts, disclosed and distinguished ([Chapter 2](#bookmark=id.g1rvfdqqc4ya), [Section 2.4](#bookmark=id.3sdtdkmqwjlq); [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.10](#bookmark=id.2c8thzi7kbd9)). The interpretive move at the centre of the thesis is an argument without authority behind it. None of these was claimed, so none of them reduces what was: a contribution that states its boundaries can be checked at them.
## **6.12 Summary**
The thesis establishes that audit-retention floors, the right to erasure and the deletion ceiling conflict only under an assumption about verifiability, and not because of the obligations themselves; that, on the broad reading of Article 68(12) and for logs kept at patient-record granularity, the conflict arises inside the European Health Data Space Regulation with no data subject acting; that a ceiling collides with a floor exactly when Proposition 3 says, and that relocation escapes the ceiling but not the right (Proposition 4). It exhibits the mechanism that dissolves the conflict and demonstrates Propositions 1 and 2 executably with an independent cross-check.
Its principal vulnerability is that the interpretive move at its centre has no regulatory authority behind it, and resolving that is the most valuable next step available. Its ceiling is that attested key destruction is not proven key destruction, a boundary marked by an active research programme in proof-of-secure-erasure and certified deletion. Its principal cost is per-record key management, bounded and auditable where the alternative’s residual-copy problem is neither. Its demonstration is a witness rather than a proof, and its synthetic records are structurally genuine but not Norwegian.
Against those, the collision is textual and, on the narrow reading of Article 68(12), survives in its erasure-driven form; the field’s own systematisation names the problem class as open; the specifications that will determine the outcome are not yet written; and the Norwegian cross-border audit stream has barely begun. [Chapter 7](#bookmark=id.suwpnvo4plx8) draws the conclusions and states the work that follows.
# **Chapter 7. Conclusion**
## **7.1 The Problem and the Answer**
This thesis began from a conflict that the European Health Data Space Regulation does not resolve. Cross-border health data exchange generates audit records subject to retention floors: ten years as reported under the eHDSI deployment baseline for MyHealth@EU audit repositories, one year under Article 73(1)(e) for the access logs of Secure Processing Environments. The same records are subject to the erasure right of Article 17 GDPR, exercisable at any moment within those windows, and to the deletion ceiling of Article 68(12) EHDS, which requires data to be gone from a Secure Processing Environment within six months of permit expiry. No instrument reconciles them, the Joint Action’s specification names their interaction as needing further guidance (TEHDAS2, 2026, Annex 7, p. 96), and the implementing acts that will have to handle them are not due until 26 March 2027.
The thesis answered the question in three movements.
It formalised the conflict as the Tri-Lateral Retention Feasibility Model, a constraint-satisfaction problem over a single binary variable per record: the accessibility of its personal-data payload. The model has three constraint types, being a parameterised retention floor, an erasure deadline, and a deletion ceiling, and it makes the semantics of *verifiability* an explicit parameter rather than an unexamined assumption.
It proved four results within that model. Under plaintext-verifiability semantics, in which a record is verifiable while its payload remains readable, the constraint system is infeasible whenever an erasure deadline or a ceiling deadline falls inside a retention window. Under accountability-preserving semantics, in which a record is verifiable while its metadata is intact, its commitment survives, and any loss of payload accessibility is itself logged and attributed, the system is jointly satisfiable for every arrival pattern of erasure requests and permit expiries and for every floor parameter. A deletion ceiling collides with a retention floor exactly when it is no longer than the floor, and its anchor decides whether the collision can be read from the text or only from each record’s history; Article 68(12), anchored to permit expiry, is of the second kind. And moving a record out of the regulated environment meets the ceiling but not the right to erasure.
It specified the mechanism that the second proof exhibits. Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation retains the accessor fields of each record and a hiding commitment, and destroys the per-record payload key, with the salt and the ciphertext, at the earlier of the erasure deadline and the deletion ceiling; for logs kept at patient-record granularity it removes the subject link at the ceiling. It appends each invalidation to a tamper-evident audit log as a first-class event carrying its month, legal ground, and authorising actor, in a log whose entries never hold what erasure reaches. At floor expiry it performs a terminal transition that destroys the identifying metadata and leaves a non-identifiable statistical residue.
The answer to the research question is therefore that the three regimes can be reconciled, that the reconciliation requires no amendment to any instrument, and that what it requires instead is abandoning an assumption about audit records that no instrument states.
## **7.2 Contributions**
Four contributions are claimed, each bounded.
*A formal characterisation of the tri-lateral retention conflict.* The general method of treating legal compliance as a satisfiability problem is established (Feng, Marsso, Sabetzadeh, & Chechik, 2023) and is not claimed here. What is new is its application to a retention system combining floors, a subject-triggered right, and a ceiling, and the isolation of verifiability semantics as the parameter that determines feasibility. The most recent systematisation of the cryptographic-erasure literature, an unreviewed preprint cited here as corroboration rather than authority, names erasure under multi-regime retention conflict among five open problems for the field (Aikebaier, 2026); this thesis addresses that problem in one regulatory setting.
*Feasibility results with an executable witness.* Proposition 1 establishes infeasibility under plaintext-verifiability semantics; Proposition 2 establishes satisfiability under the alternative and exhibits the trajectory that achieves it. Proposition 3 gives the condition under which a ceiling and a floor collide, which the cross-sector test of [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.10](#bookmark=id.odezbdc5356l) confirmed on a statute outside healthillustrated on a statute outside health (an instance generated by the thesis’s own code, which checks the code rather than independently confirming the proposition); Proposition 4 shows why relocation answers the ceiling and not the right. Both were demonstrated over two hundred records, producing ninety infeasible records and ninety-five violations under the first semantics and none under the second, with a separately written exhaustive search confirming that under the first semantics no assignment of payload accessibility whatsoever succeeds. The proofs are informal and the demonstration covers generated instances; neither is presented as more.
*A mechanism specification with its residue analysed.* The mechanism applies established primitives (cryptographic erasure as recognised in NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, hiding commitments, and, without implementing them, dynamic accumulators) and claims no cryptographic novelty. What it adds to the practitioner crypto-shredding pattern is verifiability: an auditor can establish what was invalidated, when, on what ground, and by whom, and can check each of those entries against the root of a Merkle log ([Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.7](#bookmark=id.2zhv84ggfra9)). The key hierarchy is executed with real AES-256-GCM in an optional module of the artefact. The residue it leaves is characterised as pseudonymised rather than anonymous by the Norwegian threshold, and designed to the corridor that the European Data Protection Board’s finalised Guidelines 02/2025 establish.
*An integration analysis against verified Norwegian infrastructure.* The mechanism is placed at the two narrowest points at which it achieves its purpose: the audit-repository step of the MyHealth@EU transmission flow, and the access-logging boundary of a Secure Processing Environment. It requires of the substrate nothing that the national criteria do not already demand. That constraint was derived from the documented fragmentation of Norwegian practice rather than assumed. [Table 4.1](#bookmark=id.ou2q52lu5vuw) traces the mechanism to each requirement of the regulation and of the Joint Action’s specification it touches, and places it in the activity-monitoring component of the specification’s reference architecture.
## **7.3 What the Thesis Does Not Establish**
The limitations bounding this contribution are stated canonically in [Chapter 3](#bookmark=id.6z9mt9ggf9y5), [Section 3.7](#bookmark=id.788tdzyd2un2), and engaged where they bite. They are the informal proof standard, the single-seed demonstration, the simulation of key destruction, the US Core profiles of the synthetic cohort, the unquantified operational cost of per-record key management, and the absence of regulatory authority behind two interpretive steps. They are not restated here.
Two deserve a final word because they bound the contribution rather than merely qualifying it. The invalidation entry is an attested record of destruction and not a proof of one, and no approach operating above the storage medium can supply the latter (Reardon, Basin, & Capkun, 2013). And the two interpretive steps are the subject of the next section, which states where this thesis is weakest.
## **7.4 The Two Open Questions of Authority**
Both questions are legal rather than technical, and neither can be settled by better modelling.
The first concerns verifiability. No regulator or court has held that an audit record whose payload has been cryptographically invalidated continues to satisfy a retention obligation. The thesis argues that it does, from the necessity boundary of Article 17(3)(b) read with the data-minimisation principle of Article 5(1)(c), and from the Norwegian Data Protection Authority’s own framing of retention as a balancing duty on the controller. If a supervisory authority instead reads “identifiable logs” in Article 73(1)(e) as requiring logs whose subject matter remains readable, Proposition 2 remains true of the model and inert in practice.
The second concerns scope: whether Article 68(12), which requires “the electronic health data within the secure processing environment” to be deleted within six months of permit expiry, reaches, on the broad reading, access logs kept at patient-record granularity ([Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.6](#bookmark=id.fte6am7xddnb)). Corollary 1.2 stands or falls with this question, and nothing else in the thesis does. A related question remains open on either reading: whether auditing “all processing operations” after the ceiling needs the subject link, or only the accessor fields that the Joint Action’s specification requires every log to carry.
Both questions are decidable by asking, and asking is the single highest-value action available to this research programme. A request to the competent authorities (Datatilsynet on the GDPR side; Helsedirektoratet, the Ministry of Health and Care Services or the Commission on the EHDS side) on whether accountability-preserving verifiability discharges a retention obligation, whether Article 68(12) reaches access logs kept at patient-record granularity, and whether the audit purpose of Article 73(1)(e) needs the subject link after the ceiling, has a determinate answer. A favourable answer converts the thesis’s central interpretive moves from argument into authority. An unfavourable answer refutes them cleanly and identifies precisely what would have to change. Either outcome is worth more than the present uncertainty, and neither requires further modelling to obtain.
## **7.5 Future Work**
Four lines follow, the first immediate and the remainder in ascending order of difficulty.
*Execution of the expert evaluation.* The instrument specified in Appendix C is designed and ready to execute. It comprises an eight-person panel across data protection, health IT architecture, Secure Processing Environment operation, and information logistics; a live demonstration of the artefact; a semi-structured guide; and a sixteen-item closed-response questionnaire across utility, regulatory alignment, operational viability, and audit integrity. It requires notification to Sikt and a lead time of four to six weeks, and it would supply exactly the evidence this thesis cannot generate analytically: practitioner readings of the Article 68(12) scope question, operator judgements on whether attested key destruction is sufficient in their context, and architectural assessment of the boundary placement. Together with the two authority questions of [Section 7.4](#bookmark=id.ds5sargxa3ne), this is the shortest route from the present contribution to a validated one.
*Selective disclosure of invalidation completeness.* The mechanism creates a problem it does not solve. When a data subject exercises Article 17, every record relating to them is invalidated, and an auditor should be able to confirm that *all* of them were. But identifying which records those are reveals the subject’s cross-border care history, which is precisely what the erasure was meant to protect. Proving completeness of invalidation without revealing the invalidated set is a zero-knowledge problem, and it corresponds to the fourth of the five open problems identified by Aikebaier (2026), composition with zero-knowledge selective disclosure. This is where succinct arguments become necessary rather than decorative, and the audit log of [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.8](#bookmark=id.meiwo31dw7kv) gives the problem a concrete form. If each leaf also carried a hiding commitment to its record’s subject link, a circuit taking the published root as its public input could prove that every leaf committed to a given subject is matched by an invalidation leaf, while revealing neither the leaves nor their number. Pairing-based arguments give proofs of constant size (Groth, 2016), and universal-setup systems avoid a trusted setup per circuit (Gabizon, Williamson, & Ciobotaru, 2019); which suits a regulator who must verify without trusting the controller is a design question for that work. The project name carried by this work originates in an earlier design that assumed zero-knowledge machinery would enforce the retention conflict; the analysis showed it unnecessary there, and shows it unavoidable hereand suggests it may be necessary here, though alternatives are not excluded.
*Public verifiability of deletion certificates.* The boundary identified in [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.3](#bookmark=id.wg2ajvtemzxy) would move if a deletion could be proven rather than attested. Proof-of-secure-erasure protocols pursue this in the classical setting under relaxed isolation assumptions (Bursuc, Gil-Pons, Mauw, & Trujillo-Rasua, 2024), and quantum encryption with certified deletion produces a certificate whose public verifiability its authors identify as open (Broadbent & Islam, 2020). Were public verifiability achieved, the invalidation entry specified here could carry a proof in place of an attestation, and the mechanism’s guarantee would strengthen from conditional to demonstrable with no change to the model.
*Generalisation beyond health data.* The structure the model captures (one or more retention floors, a subject-triggered erasure right, and a deletion ceiling) is not obviously specific to health, and [Chapter 6](#bookmark=id.qq702n5wmoal), [Section 6.10](#bookmark=id.odezbdc5356l) ran one test outside it: Norwegian police register law pairs a floor with a longer ceiling from the same event and, as Proposition 3 predicts, produces no collision without an erasure request. Proposition 3 turns the search for other instances into a test that can be applied to a statute’s text: look for a ceiling no longer than a floor and anchored to a different event. Applying it across regulated sectors, financial record-keeping first, would determine whether the contribution is a result about one regulation or a method for a class of them.
## **7.6 Closing**
The European Health Data Space is being built now. Norway’s National Contact Point is in live pilot at two emergency clinics, with the cross-border audit stream barely begun. The implementing acts that will specify how Secure Processing Environments handle their records are due in March 2027, and the secondary-use provisions they will operationalise apply from March 2029. The Norwegian national criteria, put to public hearing in 2025, govern how such environments are secured and who may enter them, while saying nothing about what happens when the retention regimes on their records collide.
This thesis does not claim to have found something no one could have seen. The provisions it sets against each other are public, short, and adjacent in the same chapter of the same regulation. What it claims is to have set them against each other formally, and to have shown that the resulting impossibility follows from an assumption rather than from the obligations. It claims to have exhibited and demonstrated the mechanism that dissolves it. And it claims to have done all of that while the specifications are still being written, rather than after infrastructure has hardened around the problem.
The contribution is small, bounded, and checkable. Every number in it was produced by code that runs in under a twentieth of a second and that any reader can execute. The two places where the argument outruns its authority are named, and the means of settling them is a letter rather than a research programme. What remains is to ask the questions the thesis cannot answer itself.

A note on durability. Hosted applications are not archival objects: the live demonstration may be withdrawn or may sleep after inactivity, and no claim in this thesis depends on its availability. ## **A.3 Environment and generation provenance**
The synthetic cohort was generated by the official Synthea release jar, downloaded from the project’s own GitHub releases and executed with the command in Section A.5. Generation was carried out in a Linux environment with OpenJDK 21 rather than under Windows PowerShell, which does not affect the output: Synthea is deterministic under fixed population and clinician seeds, and produces byte-identical bundles in any environment with a compatible JVM. The bundles carry Synthea’s own resource-identifier namespace, its disability-adjusted-life-years Patient extension, US Core profile conformance and its default Massachusetts demographics, all of which are verifiable by inspecting any bundle.
## **A.4 Software environment**
OS            Ubuntu 24.04
Python        3.x, standard library only (hashlib, random, itertools, glob, json, os)
Java          OpenJDK 21.0.10 (required for Synthea only)
Dependencies  none for the checker; openpyxl for the substrate patch generators
The checker has no third-party dependencies. This is deliberate: a reader should be able to run it on any machine with Python installed, without a package manager, and confirm the thesis’s central results for themselves.
## **A.5 Exact commands**
*1. Run the feasibility checker (produces every figure in *[*Chapter 5*](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1)*, *[*Sections 5.3*](#bookmark=id.ijirz43qs3c6)*–5.7):*
python3 trf\_checker.py
Deterministic. Seed 20260915 is set in the module header. Output is byte-identical across runs and across machines. Runtime measured at 0.019 s.
*2. Obtain Synthea (required only for the realism layer):*
curl -sL -o synthea.jar \\
  https://github.com/synthetichealth/synthea/releases/download/master-branch-latest/synthea-with-dependencies.jar
*3. Generate the synthetic cohort:*
mkdir -p synthea\_run && cd synthea\_run
java -jar ../synthea.jar \\
  -s 20260915 -cs 20260915 -p 100 \\
  --exporter.fhir.export=true \\
  --exporter.hospital.fhir.export=false \\
  --exporter.practitioner.fhir.export=false \\
  --generate.only\_alive\_patients=true
\-s sets the population seed and -cs the clinician seed; both are fixed to the thesis seed so the cohort is reproducible. The run yields 98 usable patient bundles from 100 requested. Output lands in synthea\_run/output/fhir/.
*4. Run the realism layer and the payload-provenance comparison (produces *[*Table 5.7*](#bookmark=id.tcfe3n4cqbml)*):*
python3 synthea\_layer.py
Looks for bundles in ./synthea\_run/output/fhir/ first and falls back to ./data/synthea\_subset/, so it runs against either the regenerated cohort or the subset shipped with the artefact. Reports both runs side by side and flags any divergence.
*5. Run the erasure-response-period witness (produces *[*Table 5.5*](#bookmark=id.z68pied0ic5p)*):*

## **A.6 What the code does**
### ***trf\_checker.py***
Implements the TRF Model of [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg) directly. Records are the seven-element tuples of [Section 4.3](#bookmark=id.b04xy7a2dxno), with the metadata split into accessor fields and subject fields. A Secure Processing Environment record carries a researcher and a permit rather than a clinician and a contact point, and its payload stands for the logged activity; a cross-border record’s payload stands for the demographic query that the IHE patient-discovery transaction puts into the audit message. Two record classes are generated: cross-border audit records with a 120-month floor, and Secure Processing Environment access-log records with a 12-month floor and the Article 68(12) ceiling. Generation parameters are listed in full in [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Table 5.2](#bookmark=id.jgvipiqoop1z).
Four components matter for the thesis’s claims:
  - check\_semantics\_I() evaluates the constraint system under plaintext verifiability, reporting for each record the first month at which C1 and C2, or C1 and C3, are simultaneously required. These are the witnesses for Proposition 1.
  - check\_semantics\_II() applies the constructive trajectory from the proof of Proposition 2 (destroy the payload key and the commitment salt and delete the payload at min(t\_r + δ, t\_π + 6); remove the subject fields of a Secure Processing Environment record at t\_π + 6; append a grounded entry for each; retain the accessor fields and the commitment) and then verifies all three constraints, including C3 over the subject link.
  - integrity() and the MerkleLog class give condition (i) of Semantics II real content. Every access event, invalidation and subject-link removal is appended to an append-only Merkle log using RFC 6962 hashing, and V\_II checks each of a record’s entries against the current root with an inclusion proof. The run includes two tamper tests, an altered accessor field and an altered invalidation ground, under which V\_II fails, and a restore after which it holds.
  - brute\_force\_semantics\_I() is written independently of the first function, taking the constraint definitions directly and enumerating all 2¹⁴ assignments of the accessibility variable over a fourteen-month horizon. It exists so that the infeasibility results do not rest on the correctness of a single implementation. The control case, in which neither C2 nor C3 is active, returns feasible: confirming the search can succeed when it should.
Cryptographic operations use hashlib only. Commitments are salted (SHA-256(salt ‖ payload)) because [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.9](#bookmark=id.bxdils4rut3s) establishes that an unsalted hash of a low-entropy clinical payload would itself remain personal data. By default make\_salt() derives each salt from the record identifier so that runs reproduce exactly; --random-salts draws them from os.urandom instead and gives the same results. The derivation is for reproducibility only: a production deployment must draw each salt from a cryptographically secure random source, since a salt derivable from the record identifier offers no hiding against an adversary who knows the derivation.
Key destruction is modelled as setting the key reference to None, and deletion of the ciphertext as setting the payload to None. This demonstrates the mechanism’s logic and demonstrates nothing about deployment assurance: a limitation stated in [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.8](#bookmark=id.nkz790ri7jg7) and treated in Chapter 6.
### ***synthea\_layer.py***
Replaces the constructed payload strings with real FHIR R4 resources drawn from Synthea bundles (one clinical resource per bundle, from Condition, Observation, MedicationRequest, AllergyIntolerance, Immunization, or Procedure), recomputes each commitment over the real payload, and leaves every timing quantity untouched. It then runs both populations through the same checks and prints them side by side.
The expected result, and the observed one, is that every reported figure is identical while all 200 commitments differ. Mean payload size rises from 43 bytes to 891 with the committed subset (to 1,006 with the full cohort, recorded on 28 September when the constructed payloads averaged 35 bytes; see A.17). The model reads timing and accessibility, never payload content; running the comparison rather than asserting the invariance lets a reader see the claim tested against inputs that demonstrably changed.
## **A.7 Data provenance**
All data used anywhere in this thesis is synthetic. No real patient data was requested, obtained, or processed at any point.
The cohort is generated by Synthea (Walonoski et al., 2018), an open-source synthetic patient generator. Synthea’s default export conforms to the *US Core* implementation guide with United States demographic, geographic, and care-pattern parameters. The FHIR version is *R4*, which matches the version the Norwegian basisprofiler constrain; the *profiles* are not Norwegian, and no claim of Norwegian clinical representativeness is made for these records. The invariance result of [Table 5.7](#bookmark=id.tcfe3n4cqbml) establishes that this mismatch cannot affect any reported figure. The thesis’s Norwegian grounding rests on the infrastructure analysis of [Chapter 4](#bookmark=id.vcjx7jgm2aqg), [Section 4.11](#bookmark=id.44y1dgcnl0qq).
The eight bundles in data/synthea\_subset/ are untrimmed output from that cohort. With the subset the mean payload is 891 bytes rather than the 1,006 bytes of the full cohort, because a different set of clinical resources is drawn; [Chapter 5](#bookmark=id.6c65wl28gfw1), [Section 5.8](#bookmark=id.nkz790ri7jg7) reports both and every other figure is identical.
